genai.title: Setup + Your First LLM Call
objectives: Python venv + keys the safe way
Call an LLM from Python and Java (Spring AI)
Read token usage, cost, and determinism
interviewFocus: Explain a first LLM call end-to-end
Secrets handling: env vars / .env, never in code

questions.text: Why do we keep API keys in an environment variable or a gitignored .env file instead of hard-coding them?
keyPoints: secrets must never be committed to git
separates config from code
lets you rotate keys without code changes
.env is gitignored so it stays out of the repo

questions.text: What does a Python virtual environment (venv) give you?
keyPoints: an isolated set of dependencies per project
avoids polluting the system Python
reproducible installs without version clashes

questions.text: Give one situation where you'd use Java/Spring AI for an LLM feature, and one where you'd use Python.
keyPoints: Java/Spring AI: embedding LLM into an existing JVM/Spring production backend
Python: the AI-first library ecosystem / fast prototyping / newest tools land there first

questions.text: What does the 'usage' object in an LLM API response tell you, and why does it matter?
keyPoints: a breakdown of prompt tokens, completion tokens, and total tokens for that call
lets you compute the exact cost of the call since pricing is per-token
essential for monitoring and budgeting once a feature is in production

questions.text: At a high level, what does a Spring AI ChatClient call do under the hood?
keyPoints: builds a request in Spring AI's provider-agnostic shape
Spring AI translates it into the specific format the configured provider (OpenAI, Groq, etc.) expects
returns a ChatResponse wrapping the generated message plus metadata like token usage

questions.text: Why might the exact same prompt cost a different amount on two separate calls?
keyPoints: generation is non-deterministic, so completion length (and thus output tokens) can vary between runs
if the model or provider changed between calls, per-token pricing can differ
cost = input tokens + output tokens, and only the output side is inherently variable

genai.title: LLM Fundamentals & Prompting
objectives: System vs user messages, structured output

questions.text: Why is an LLM call's token count higher than the number of words in your message?
keyPoints: tokens include the role/formatting scaffolding (system/user markers), not just your words
tokenization splits text into sub-word pieces
punctuation and spaces also count as tokens

questions.text: What does the 'temperature' setting control, and what do higher vs lower values do?
keyPoints: controls the randomness of token sampling, NOT accuracy or correctness
low = focused, repeatable, near-deterministic
high = more varied and creative
it reshapes the probability distribution before sampling

questions.text: You pay per token in two buckets — name both, and say which is usually priced higher.
keyPoints: input / prompt tokens
output / completion tokens
output tokens are priced higher

questions.text: Mechanically, why can the exact same prompt return different text on different runs?
keyPoints: the model produces a probability distribution over the next token
it samples (a weighted random draw) instead of always the top token
so runs diverge

questions.text: What is a system message vs a user message, and when would you use a system message?
keyPoints: user = the end-user's actual request
system = standing instructions/persona/rules/format for the whole conversation
use system to set behavior or output format

questions.text: When would you choose RAG over plain prompting, and over fine-tuning?
keyPoints: RAG when answers need external/private/up-to-date facts grounded in your documents
prompting for tasks within the model's general knowledge
fine-tuning to change style/format/behavior at scale, not to inject facts

questions.text: What is the context window, and what happens when a conversation exceeds it?
keyPoints: the maximum number of tokens (input + output combined) the model can process in one call
exceeding it either truncates/drops older context or causes the call to error, depending on the client
a longer context isn't free — cost and latency both scale with how much you send

questions.text: How do you get an LLM to reliably return valid, parseable JSON instead of freeform prose?
keyPoints: use the provider's structured-output/JSON mode or function/tool calling rather than just asking nicely in the prompt
as a fallback, give an explicit schema/example in the prompt
always parse defensively — even structured-output modes can occasionally produce malformed output

questions.text: What is an embedding, and how does semantic search use it to find relevant text?
keyPoints: text is converted to a vector that captures meaning
similar meaning -> nearby vectors
the query is embedded and nearest-neighbor search returns the closest chunks

questions.text: cosine similarity vs L2 distance — what's the difference and which is common for text embeddings?
keyPoints: cosine compares direction/angle (magnitude-insensitive)
L2 is straight-line distance
cosine is common for text embeddings

questions.text: HNSW vs IVFFlat index — what's the trade-off?
keyPoints: both are approximate nearest-neighbor indexes
HNSW: graph-based, high recall/speed, more memory & build cost
IVFFlat: cluster-based, cheaper/faster to build, tune probes for recall

questions.text: Why not just use SQL LIKE or full-text search instead of vector search?
keyPoints: keyword search misses paraphrases and meaning
vectors match semantic similarity
hybrid search combines keyword + vector for the best of both

questions.text: Why does chunk size matter for RAG retrieval quality?
keyPoints: small chunks give precise retrieval but can lose the surrounding context a passage needs to make sense
large chunks preserve more context but dilute relevance — a match on one sentence pulls in a lot of unrelated text
overlapping chunk boundaries helps avoid splitting one relevant idea across two separate chunks

questions.text: Does a higher-dimensional embedding always mean better search quality?
keyPoints: dimensionality is fixed per embedding model (e.g., 384/768/1536) and isn't something you tune per query
no — higher dimensionality trades off storage and compute cost against often-marginal quality gains
the right model/dimensionality depends on the specific domain and scale, not just 'bigger is better'

genai.title: RAG End-to-End
interviewFocus: Design a RAG system for private docs

questions.text: Walk through the stages of a RAG pipeline in order.
keyPoints: ingest -> chunk -> embed -> store (index)
retrieve (optionally re-rank)
augment the prompt with retrieved context
generate the answer, ideally with citations

questions.text: How does RAG reduce hallucination, and when does it still fail?
keyPoints: it grounds the answer in retrieved, cited context
fails if retrieval misses the relevant docs
or if the model ignores the provided context

questions.text: What is hybrid search and why use it?
keyPoints: combine vector (semantic) with keyword/BM25 search
catches paraphrase AND exact terms like IDs/code
scores from both are merged

questions.text: How do you evaluate RAG quality and catch a regression before shipping?
keyPoints: an eval set scoring faithfulness/relevance/answer-correctness
run it in CI as a gate
golden question/answer pairs

questions.text: What does a re-ranker do in a RAG pipeline, and why run one after initial retrieval instead of just fetching more documents?
keyPoints: a re-ranker is a more accurate (and more expensive) relevance model applied to a small candidate set
initial retrieval (vector or hybrid search) is fast but approximate; re-ranking refines the top-k for precision
running the expensive re-ranking model over the ENTIRE corpus instead of a small candidate set would be too slow/costly

questions.text: How do you add citations to a RAG answer, and why does that matter?
keyPoints: track which source chunk each part of the generated answer actually drew from
surface those sources alongside the answer so the user can verify claims
citations also help YOU debug retrieval failures when an answer looks wrong

resources.title: Functions, Tools and Agents with LangChain

questions.text: In LLM tool-calling, who actually runs the tool — the model or your code?
keyPoints: the model outputs a request to call a named function with arguments
YOUR code executes the tool
the result is fed back to the model; the model does not run code itself

questions.text: What is the agent reason-act-observe loop, and when is an agent the wrong choice?
keyPoints: reason -> call a tool (act) -> observe result -> repeat
wrong when a simple deterministic chain suffices
agents add cost, latency, and unpredictability

questions.text: How do you stop an agent from looping forever and burning tokens/cost?
keyPoints: a max step/iteration limit
a token/cost budget or timeout
guardrails on tool use

questions.text: What does MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardize?
keyPoints: a standard protocol/interface for connecting LLMs to tools and data sources
replaces bespoke per-integration glue with a common client-server contract

questions.text: What's the difference between a single tool call and a full agent loop?
keyPoints: a single tool call is one request -> one function execution -> one response, with no iteration
an agent loop repeats reason -> act -> observe multiple times, deciding at each step whether to call another tool or finish
agents are needed when a task requires several dependent steps chosen dynamically, not a single fixed action

questions.text: Give a concrete example of what an MCP server exposes to an LLM client.
keyPoints: an MCP server exposes resources, tools, and/or prompts over the standard protocol
example: a GitHub MCP server exposing tools to read files, list issues, or open a PR
the LLM client (host app) discovers and calls these capabilities without bespoke per-integration code

questions.text: What is prompt injection, and give two concrete mitigations.
keyPoints: malicious input that overrides your instructions or exfiltrates data
separate/treat user input as untrusted; validate model output
least-privilege tools; never blindly execute model output; guardrails

questions.text: How do you test something non-deterministic like an LLM feature?
keyPoints: eval sets scored by metrics or LLM-as-judge
assert on properties/rubrics not exact strings
golden datasets with thresholds, run in CI

questions.text: Name three levers to cut LLM latency or cost in production.
keyPoints: caching (exact and/or semantic)
route easy calls to a cheaper/smaller model
shorter prompts/context; batching; streaming for perceived latency

questions.text: What should you log for an LLM app, and what must you NOT log?
keyPoints: log prompts/responses, tokens, cost, latency for observability
do NOT log secrets or PII (redact them)

questions.text: What's the difference between exact-match caching and semantic caching for LLM calls?
keyPoints: exact-match caching only hits when the request is literally identical to a prior one
semantic caching matches semantically similar prior queries (via embedding similarity) even if worded differently
semantic caching catches more cache hits but risks an occasional false-positive match returning a slightly wrong cached answer

questions.text: Why is 'LLM-as-judge' a common evaluation technique, and what's a real risk of relying on it?
keyPoints: a strong LLM grades another LLM's output at scale — much cheaper and faster than human review
risk: the judge model has its own biases/blind spots and can be fooled by confident-sounding but wrong answers
judge scores should be periodically validated against real human judgment, not trusted blindly

genai.title: Capstone — RAG Assistant
interviewFocus: Why X not Y for chunking/index/model

questions.text: For your RAG app, justify your chunk size and index choice, and what you'd change at 10x scale.
keyPoints: chunk size trades retrieval granularity vs context dilution
index choice (HNSW/IVFFlat) trades recall/speed vs memory/build
at scale: sharding, caching, cost controls, monitoring

questions.text: How would you add cost controls and evaluation to your capstone?
keyPoints: caching, cheaper-model routing, per-session budgets
an eval set (faithfulness/relevance) run in CI

questions.text: What are the key steps to deploy a Spring Boot GenAI app to AWS, and what's one concern specific to LLM-backed services?
keyPoints: containerize the app (Docker) and deploy via ECS/EKS or a simpler PaaS like Elastic Beanstalk
manage API keys/secrets through a secrets manager, never in env files baked into the image
LLM-specific concern: rate limiting and cost control against a third-party API, plus handling provider timeouts/retries gracefully

questions.text: In a 5-minute architecture walkthrough of your capstone, what should you cover, and in what order?
keyPoints: start with the problem/user need, not the tech stack
then the high-level data flow (ingest -> store -> retrieve -> generate)
then your 2-3 most defensible design decisions, then a known limitation you'd fix next

questions.text: What's one thing you'd change about your capstone to support 10x the current traffic?
keyPoints: identify the ACTUAL bottleneck (usually the vector index or the LLM call itself) rather than scaling everything uniformly
cache aggressively and scale the stateless app tier horizontally
consider routing high-volume/easy queries to a cheaper, faster model with fallback to a stronger model for hard cases

questions.text: When would you use a hash map instead of sorting to solve a problem, and what's the time/space trade-off?
keyPoints: hash map gives O(1) average lookup -> often O(n) time but O(n) extra space
sorting is O(n log n) time with little/no extra space
use hashing when you need fast membership/counts and can afford the space

questions.text: What does Big-O notation describe, and why do interviews focus on the worst case?
keyPoints: asymptotic growth of time/space as input grows; constants are ignored
worst case gives a guaranteed upper bound regardless of input

questions.text: Give an example where a hash set turns an O(n^2) solution into O(n).
keyPoints: e.g. two-sum or detecting duplicates
store seen elements and check the complement/existence in O(1)

questions.text: What's the difference between average-case and worst-case complexity for a HashMap, and when does the worst case happen?
keyPoints: average O(1) assumes a reasonable hash function spreading keys evenly across buckets
worst case O(n) (or O(log n) in Java 8+ with treeification) happens when many keys collide into the same bucket
a poor or adversarially-chosen hashCode can trigger this

questions.text: Why is string concatenation inside a loop often a hidden O(n^2) trap, and how do you avoid it?
keyPoints: each concatenation typically creates a NEW string, copying every prior character
doing this n times in a loop is O(n^2) total work, not O(n)
use a mutable builder (StringBuilder, or a list joined once at the end) to get true O(n)

questions.text: Given two arrays, what's the fastest way to check whether they share any element, and why?
keyPoints: put one array's elements into a hash set — O(n) to build
check membership for each element of the second array — O(m)
overall O(n+m), versus the naive nested-loop comparison's O(n*m)

questions.text: What signals in a problem suggest a sliding-window approach?
keyPoints: a contiguous subarray/substring
finding the longest/shortest/optimal window meeting a condition
avoids recomputation by expanding/shrinking the window

questions.text: How does a variable-size sliding window achieve O(n) instead of O(n^2)?
keyPoints: each element enters and leaves the window at most once
both pointers only move forward

questions.text: Two pointers vs sliding window — when would you use each?
keyPoints: two pointers: often sorted arrays / both ends (pair sums, partitioning)
sliding window: optimize over a contiguous range

questions.text: In a sliding-window problem, what determines whether you shrink the window from the left?
keyPoints: shrink whenever the current window violates the problem's constraint (too many distinct chars, sum too large, etc.)
shrink until the constraint is satisfied again, then resume expanding from the right

questions.text: Give an example of a two-pointer problem where the pointers start at OPPOSITE ends rather than both at the start.
keyPoints: e.g. 'container with most water' or two-sum on a sorted array
one pointer starts at index 0, the other at the last index, moving inward based on a comparison — exploiting the sorted/structured input

questions.text: Why do two-pointer and sliding-window techniques typically require some structure in the input, like being sorted?
keyPoints: they rely on being able to make a monotonic decision about which pointer to move next
on unstructured input you often need to sort first (adding O(n log n)) or fall back to a different technique like hashing

questions.text: Give a problem where a stack is the natural fit, and why.
keyPoints: matching parentheses / monotonic stack / undo
LIFO — the most recent item is what you need next

questions.text: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list, and what's the complexity?
keyPoints: Floyd's fast & slow pointers
O(n) time, O(1) space; the pointers meet inside the cycle

questions.text: Array vs linked list — the key trade-offs?
keyPoints: array: O(1) index access, contiguous, costly mid insert/delete
linked list: O(1) insert/delete at a node, O(n) access, extra pointer memory

questions.text: How do you reverse a singly linked list iteratively, and what's the space complexity?
keyPoints: walk the list maintaining prev/curr/next pointers, reversing each link as you go
O(n) time, O(1) space
a recursive approach would instead be O(n) space due to the call stack

questions.text: What's a monotonic stack, and give a problem it solves efficiently.
keyPoints: a stack kept in strictly increasing or decreasing order by popping elements that violate the order before pushing
classic use: 'next greater element' — solved in O(n) instead of the naive O(n^2)

questions.text: Queue vs Deque — when do you need a deque instead of a plain queue?
keyPoints: a plain queue only allows enqueue at one end and dequeue at the other (FIFO)
a deque allows insertion/removal at BOTH ends
needed for problems like sliding-window maximum, where you must remove from either end efficiently

questions.text: What property makes BST search O(log n), and when does it degrade to O(n)?
keyPoints: left < root < right ordering enables binary search
degrades to O(n) when the tree is unbalanced/skewed; balanced trees (AVL/Red-Black) keep O(log n)

questions.text: BFS vs DFS traversal of a tree — difference and when to use each?
keyPoints: BFS = level-order (queue), good for shortest path / level info
DFS = deep (stack/recursion), good for path/subtree problems, less memory on wide trees

questions.text: How would you check whether a binary tree is a valid BST?
keyPoints: in-order traversal must be strictly increasing, OR recurse carrying min/max bounds
a simple parent-child check is not sufficient

questions.text: How do you find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two nodes in a BST, using the BST property?
keyPoints: start at the root; if both target values are less than the current node, go left; if both greater, go right
the first node where the values diverge (one <=, one >) is the LCA
O(h) time, where h is the tree's height

questions.text: What's the difference between a balanced and an unbalanced binary tree, and why does it matter when you state complexity?
keyPoints: balanced means height is O(log n) relative to the number of nodes
unbalanced can degrade to O(n) height — effectively a linked list
always state which case (balanced vs worst-case skewed) your complexity claim assumes

questions.text: How would you serialize and deserialize a binary tree?
keyPoints: a common approach: pre-order traversal, writing an explicit marker for missing (null) children
deserialize by reading tokens in the same order and reconstructing recursively

questions.text: Adjacency list vs adjacency matrix — trade-offs?
keyPoints: list: O(V+E) space, efficient for sparse graphs
matrix: O(V^2) space, O(1) edge lookup, better for dense graphs

questions.text: When do you use BFS vs DFS on a graph?
keyPoints: BFS: shortest path in an unweighted graph, level exploration
DFS: cycle detection, topological sort, connectivity, path existence

questions.text: How do you avoid infinite loops when traversing a graph?
keyPoints: keep a visited set/array and mark nodes as you go
graphs can have cycles, unlike trees

questions.text: What's topological sort, and what precondition must a graph satisfy for it to exist?
keyPoints: an ordering of nodes such that every directed edge points from an earlier node to a later one
only exists for a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) — a cycle makes a valid topological order impossible

questions.text: How does Dijkstra's algorithm find shortest paths, and why does it fail with negative edge weights?
keyPoints: greedily expands the closest unvisited node using a priority queue, relaxing edges as it goes
it assumes once a node's shortest distance is finalized it can't improve
a later negative edge could still shorten a path, breaking that assumption

questions.text: What problem does Union-Find (Disjoint Set) solve efficiently, and what's one optimization that speeds it up?
keyPoints: efficiently tracks and merges groups of connected components, answering 'are these two nodes connected' quickly
path compression and union by rank/size bring operations to near-O(1) amortized

questions.text: What signals that a problem can be solved with dynamic programming?
keyPoints: overlapping subproblems AND optimal substructure
the same subproblems recur and can be cached/reused

questions.text: Memoization vs tabulation — what's the difference?
keyPoints: memoization: top-down recursion with a cache
tabulation: bottom-up iterative table; both remove recomputation

questions.text: How does memoization change naive recursive Fibonacci's complexity?
keyPoints: naive is O(2^n) exponential
memoized is O(n) time and O(n) space by caching subresults

questions.text: What's the time/space complexity of a typical bottom-up DP solution with a 2D table, and how can you often reduce the space?
keyPoints: O(rows*cols) time and space for the full table
if each row/state only depends on the PREVIOUS row, roll the table down to O(cols) space by keeping just the last row (or two)

questions.text: How do you identify the 'state' in a DP problem?
keyPoints: the state is the minimal set of parameters that uniquely determines a subproblem's answer (e.g., index + remaining capacity for knapsack)
getting the state definition right is usually the hardest part of solving a new DP problem

questions.text: Give an example of a greedy approach failing where DP succeeds, and explain why.
keyPoints: e.g. coin change with non-canonical denominations — greedily picking the largest coin each time doesn't always give the optimal count
DP explores all valid combinations and keeps the best; greedy commits early without reconsidering

questions.text: Vertical vs horizontal scaling — the trade-offs?
keyPoints: vertical = bigger machine: simple but limited/expensive, single point of failure
horizontal = more machines: scales far but needs load balancing and stateless servers

questions.text: What does a load balancer do, and why is statelessness important behind it?
keyPoints: distributes traffic across servers
stateless servers let any server handle any request (session in shared store), enabling scale and failover

questions.text: Define latency and throughput, and give a trade-off between them.
keyPoints: latency = time per request; throughput = requests per second
batching can raise throughput but increase per-request latency

questions.text: Name two load balancing algorithms and how they differ.
keyPoints: round robin: cycles through servers evenly, ignoring current load
least connections: routes to the server with the fewest active connections — better when requests cost unevenly
consistent hashing: routes based on a key so the same client/data tends to hit the same server, useful for caching

questions.text: What's a single point of failure, and how does horizontal scaling with a load balancer address it?
keyPoints: a component whose failure takes down the whole system
running multiple server instances behind a load balancer means one instance failing doesn't take the service down — traffic routes to the survivors

questions.text: Why do back-of-envelope scale estimates matter before you start designing?
keyPoints: they reveal whether you're designing for thousands or billions of requests, which drives fundamentally different architecture choices
skipping this leads to either over-engineering a small system or under-engineering one that actually needs to scale

questions.text: When would you choose NoSQL over a relational database?
keyPoints: flexible/large-scale/denormalized data, high write throughput, easy horizontal scaling, few complex joins
choose SQL for strong consistency, relations, and ACID transactions

questions.text: Sharding vs replication — what does each solve?
keyPoints: sharding splits data across nodes for scale / write throughput
replication copies data for read scaling and availability/failover

questions.text: State the CAP theorem in one sentence, with a practical implication.
keyPoints: under a network partition you must choose consistency or availability
e.g. pick AP (eventual consistency) or CP depending on the use case

questions.text: What's a database index, and what's the trade-off of adding one?
keyPoints: a separate data structure (commonly a B-tree) that speeds up lookups on a column without scanning the whole table
trade-off: extra storage, and slower writes since every index must also be updated on insert/update/delete

questions.text: Explain eventual consistency with a concrete example.
keyPoints: after a write, different replicas may temporarily return different (stale) values until they converge
example: a 'like' count that briefly shows different numbers to different users right after a like, then settles to the same value

questions.text: How would you design a schema to avoid the N+1 query problem at the database/query-design level?
keyPoints: denormalize selectively (embed frequently-needed related data) where read performance matters more than write simplicity
or ensure the query layer uses joins/batch fetches instead of one query per row
the goal is minimizing round trips, whether through schema design or query pattern

questions.text: Why cache, and name a hard problem caching introduces.
keyPoints: reduces latency and DB load
cache invalidation is hard — stale data, TTL vs write-through/write-back trade-offs

questions.text: What problem does a message queue solve?
keyPoints: decouples producers from consumers
smooths load spikes and enables async processing, retries, and resilience

questions.text: Cache-aside vs write-through — what's the difference?
keyPoints: cache-aside: app loads on miss, writes DB then invalidates cache
write-through: write cache and DB together — fresher reads, higher write latency

questions.text: What's the difference between at-least-once and exactly-once delivery in a message queue, and why is exactly-once so hard?
keyPoints: at-least-once may redeliver a message after a failure, so the consumer must handle duplicates / be idempotent
exactly-once requires coordinating message delivery with the consumer's processing atomically
true exactly-once is expensive and rarely fully guaranteed end-to-end across distributed systems

questions.text: When would you choose a write-back (write-behind) cache strategy, and what risk does it introduce?
keyPoints: write to cache immediately and asynchronously flush to the database later — lowest possible write latency
risk: data loss if the cache fails before the flush to the database happens

questions.text: What's cache stampede (thundering herd), and how do you prevent it?
keyPoints: many requests simultaneously miss a just-expired cache entry and all hit the database at once
prevented with request coalescing (only one request repopulates the cache, others wait), staggered TTLs, or a lock around repopulation

questions.text: Monolith vs microservices — the key trade-offs?
keyPoints: monolith: simpler to build/deploy but harder to scale teams and parts independently
microservices: independent scaling/deploy but network complexity, data consistency, and ops overhead

questions.text: Why and how do you rate-limit an API?
keyPoints: protect from abuse/overload, ensure fairness, control cost
algorithms like token bucket or leaky bucket, applied per API key/user

questions.text: Name two resilience patterns for service-to-service calls and what they prevent.
keyPoints: timeouts and retries with backoff
circuit breaker (stop calling a failing service), bulkhead, fallback

questions.text: What's an API gateway, and what does it centralize in a microservices architecture?
keyPoints: the single entry point clients call, which routes each request to the correct backend service
centralizes auth, rate limiting, logging, and sometimes response aggregation, so individual services don't reimplement them

questions.text: What's the Saga pattern, and what problem does it solve?
keyPoints: manages a business transaction spanning multiple microservices/databases, where a single ACID transaction isn't possible
breaks it into local transactions with explicit compensating actions to undo prior steps if a later step fails

questions.text: How do you handle service discovery when instances scale up/down dynamically?
keyPoints: a service registry (e.g. Consul, Eureka, or a cloud-native equivalent) that services register with on startup and deregister on shutdown
callers/load balancers query the registry instead of hardcoding instance addresses

questions.text: Sketch the high-level components of a RAG system.
keyPoints: ingestion: chunk -> embed -> store in a vector DB
retrieval (optionally re-rank) -> augment the prompt -> LLM generates
plus caching, evals, and guardrails

questions.text: What does an LLM gateway do in production?
keyPoints: a central layer for caching, model routing (cheap vs strong), rate limiting, retries/fallback
and cost/usage tracking + key management

questions.text: How would you scale a vector DB to 100M vectors with low latency?
keyPoints: an ANN index (HNSW/IVF)
sharding/partitioning + read replicas, cache hot queries, tune the recall/latency trade-off

questions.text: How would you design rate limiting for an LLM-backed API, where cost varies wildly per request?
keyPoints: token-based limiting, not just request-count — a request with a huge context costs far more than a short one
per-user/per-key budgets tracked against actual token usage rather than raw request counts

questions.text: What fallback strategy would you design for when your primary LLM provider is down or rate-limited?
keyPoints: a secondary provider/model as a fallback, accepting a possible quality trade-off
or a cached/degraded response when no live generation is possible
a circuit breaker to stop hammering a failing provider and fail over quickly

questions.text: How would you keep a RAG system's knowledge fresh without re-embedding the entire document store on every update?
keyPoints: incremental indexing — only re-embed and update the changed/added documents, not the whole corpus
track document versions/timestamps to know exactly what needs re-processing

questions.text: How does a HashMap work internally, and what happens on a hash collision?
keyPoints: keys are hashed to a bucket index; Java 8+ uses a linked list per bucket that treeifies into a red-black tree once a bucket gets large enough
collisions are resolved by chaining within the bucket
resizing (rehashing) happens once the load factor threshold is exceeded

questions.text: ArrayList vs LinkedList — when would you choose each?
keyPoints: ArrayList: O(1) index access, O(n) insert/remove in the middle, contiguous/cache-friendly
LinkedList: O(1) insert/remove given a node reference, O(n) access by index, more memory overhead per element
ArrayList is the default choice for most cases; LinkedList rarely wins in practice on modern hardware

questions.text: What's the difference between synchronized, a ReentrantLock, and using java.util.concurrent classes like ConcurrentHashMap?
keyPoints: synchronized: simplest, JVM-managed, coarse-grained, no timeout/tryLock ability
ReentrantLock: explicit lock/unlock, supports tryLock/timeouts/fairness, more flexible but must be unlocked in a finally block
ConcurrentHashMap: lock-striped/lock-free concurrent data structure — usually the right choice over manually synchronizing a HashMap

questions.text: What triggers a garbage collection, and what's the difference between minor and major/full GC?
keyPoints: objects are collected when no longer reachable from GC roots
minor GC: cleans the young generation, frequent and fast
major/full GC: cleans the old generation (or the whole heap), less frequent but much more expensive/pausing

questions.text: What's type erasure in Java generics, and what's one practical consequence of it?
keyPoints: generic type parameters are erased to their bound (or Object) at compile time — they don't exist at runtime
consequence: you can't do `new T()` or `instanceof T`, and you can't overload methods that differ only by generic type parameter

questions.text: What's a functional interface, and how does a lambda expression relate to it?
keyPoints: an interface with exactly ONE abstract method (e.g. Runnable, Comparator, or a custom @FunctionalInterface)
a lambda expression is essentially syntactic sugar providing an inline implementation of that single abstract method

javafs.title: Spring & Spring Boot Fundamentals
interviewFocus: How auto-configuration decides what to wire

questions.text: What is dependency injection, and why does Spring favor constructor injection over field injection?
keyPoints: DI means an object's dependencies are provided externally rather than created internally, decoupling components
constructor injection makes dependencies explicit/immutable/required, enables easier testing (no reflection needed), and fails fast at startup if a dependency is missing
field injection hides dependencies, allows partially-constructed objects, and complicates unit testing

questions.text: Explain the Spring bean lifecycle at a high level.
keyPoints: instantiate -> populate properties/inject dependencies -> call Aware interfaces -> BeanPostProcessors (before) -> @PostConstruct/InitializingBean -> bean ready for use -> @PreDestroy/DisposableBean on shutdown
understanding this matters for correctly hooking initialization/cleanup logic

questions.text: How does Spring Boot's auto-configuration decide what to configure?
keyPoints: @ConditionalOnClass/@ConditionalOnMissingBean/@ConditionalOnProperty etc. gate each auto-configuration class
it inspects the classpath and existing bean definitions, only activating configuration when its conditions are met
this is why adding a dependency (e.g., a JDBC driver) can automatically wire up related beans

questions.text: Singleton vs prototype bean scope — what's the difference and a case for each?
keyPoints: singleton (default): one shared instance per Spring container — fine for stateless services
prototype: a new instance every time the bean is requested — used for stateful, non-thread-safe objects

questions.text: What are Spring profiles, and how do you activate one?
keyPoints: profiles let you define environment-specific beans/configuration (dev, test, prod)
activate via the spring.profiles.active property, an environment variable, or programmatically
a bean annotated @Profile("x") only loads when that profile is active

questions.text: What is AOP, and give a real example of it already at work inside Spring itself.
keyPoints: Aspect-Oriented Programming factors cross-cutting concerns (logging, security, transactions) out into reusable aspects applied via pointcuts
@Transactional itself is implemented as AOP advice that wraps a method call in a transaction begin/commit/rollback

questions.text: What is the N+1 query problem, and how do you fix it?
keyPoints: fetching a list of N entities, then lazily fetching a related entity for EACH one triggers 1 + N queries instead of one efficient query
fix with a JOIN FETCH in JPQL, an @EntityGraph, or batch fetching, to retrieve related data in one (or few) queries

questions.text: Explain @Transactional propagation levels — REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW.
keyPoints: REQUIRED (default): joins an existing transaction if one exists, or creates a new one
REQUIRES_NEW: always suspends any existing transaction and starts a new, independent one — a rollback in the outer transaction won't undo what REQUIRES_NEW already committed

questions.text: What causes a LazyInitializationException, and how do you avoid it?
keyPoints: accessing a lazily-loaded association after the persistence session/transaction that fetched the entity has closed
fix by fetching eagerly when needed (JOIN FETCH), keeping the access within the transactional boundary, or using a DTO projection instead of the raw entity

questions.text: Lazy vs eager fetching in JPA — what's the trade-off, and what's the default for @OneToMany vs @ManyToOne?
keyPoints: lazy loads the association only when accessed (saves memory/query cost, but risks LazyInitializationException outside a session)
eager always loads it immediately (simpler, but can over-fetch and hurt performance)
@OneToMany/@ManyToMany default to lazy; @ManyToOne/@OneToOne default to eager

questions.text: Name the standard transaction isolation levels and what each additionally prevents over the one below it.
keyPoints: READ_UNCOMMITTED: prevents nothing (dirty reads possible)
READ_COMMITTED: prevents dirty reads
REPEATABLE_READ: also prevents non-repeatable reads
SERIALIZABLE: also prevents phantom reads — each stronger level trades concurrency/performance for consistency

questions.text: What are the JPA entity lifecycle states, and what triggers the transition from transient to persistent?
keyPoints: transient (new, not yet associated with a persistence context) -> persistent (managed, changes tracked) -> detached (was managed, session closed) -> removed
calling entityManager.persist() (or repository.save() on a new entity) transitions it from transient to persistent

javafs.title: REST APIs, Validation & Security
interviewFocus: Design a clean REST error response
CORS vs CSRF — what each protects against

questions.text: How do you handle exceptions cleanly across a Spring Boot REST API?
keyPoints: a centralized @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods mapping exceptions to consistent error responses (status code, message, timestamp)
avoids scattering try/catch blocks across controllers and keeps error responses consistent for API consumers

questions.text: JWT-based auth vs traditional session-based auth — what's the trade-off?
keyPoints: JWT: stateless, the token itself carries the claims, scales horizontally without shared session storage, but harder to revoke before expiry
session-based: server holds state (in-memory or shared store), easy to revoke immediately, but needs sticky sessions or a shared session store to scale

questions.text: What's the difference between CORS and CSRF, and what does each protect against?
keyPoints: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing): a browser mechanism controlling which origins are ALLOWED to call your API from client-side JS
CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery): an attack where a malicious site tricks a logged-in user's browser into making an unwanted request; defended with CSRF tokens or SameSite cookies
CORS is about permission to call; CSRF protection is about proving the request was intentional

questions.text: How do you version a REST API, and what are the trade-offs of common approaches?
keyPoints: URI versioning (/api/v1/...): simple, visible, but can lead to code duplication
header/content-negotiation versioning: cleaner URIs but less discoverable and harder to test manually
the choice depends on how many consumers you have and how often breaking changes occur

questions.text: How do you validate an incoming request body in a Spring Boot controller, and what happens automatically on failure?
keyPoints: annotate the DTO fields with Bean Validation annotations (@NotNull, @Size, @Email, etc.) and the controller parameter with @Valid
a failure throws MethodArgumentNotValidException before the method body runs, which Spring Boot's default handling turns into a 400 response

questions.text: What does the OAuth2 authorization code flow protect against that the older implicit flow didn't?
keyPoints: the access token exchange happens server-to-server using a confidential client secret, rather than the token being returned directly to the browser
this keeps the long-lived, powerful access token out of browser history, referrer headers, and JS-accessible storage

javafs.title: Testing (JUnit, Mockito, Integration)
interviewFocus: Why testcontainers over an in-memory DB for integration tests

questions.text: What's the difference between a unit test and an integration test, and where's the boundary?
keyPoints: unit test: tests one class/method in isolation, dependencies mocked, fast, no Spring context
integration test: verifies multiple components working together (e.g., a real DB, the Spring context), slower but catches wiring/config issues unit tests miss

questions.text: Mock vs spy in Mockito — what's the difference?
keyPoints: mock: a fully fake object with no real behavior unless stubbed
spy: wraps a REAL object, calling real methods by default unless specific methods are stubbed — useful for partial mocking

questions.text: Why use Testcontainers instead of an in-memory database (like H2) for integration tests?
keyPoints: an in-memory DB can behave differently from your real production database (SQL dialect quirks, feature gaps)
Testcontainers spins up the REAL database engine (e.g., actual Postgres) in Docker for the test, giving much higher confidence the tests reflect production behavior

questions.text: What does @SpringBootTest do, and why would you use a narrower test slice like @WebMvcTest instead?
keyPoints: @SpringBootTest loads the full application context — thorough but slow
@WebMvcTest (or @DataJpaTest, etc.) loads only the relevant slice of the context — much faster, appropriate when you're only testing one layer

questions.text: What does @MockBean do differently from a plain Mockito.mock() call inside a Spring test?
keyPoints: @MockBean replaces the real bean of that type INSIDE the Spring application context, so other autowired beans transparently receive the mock
a plain Mockito.mock() is just a local object you construct and wire yourself — it never touches the Spring context, making it the faster choice for a pure unit test

questions.text: Why does Spring's TestContext framework cache the ApplicationContext between test classes, and what can accidentally break that caching?
keyPoints: starting a full Spring context is expensive; caching it (keyed by its exact configuration) lets many test classes share one instead of rebuilding it repeatedly
a different @ActiveProfiles or a different set of @MockBean overrides between test classes changes the cache key, forcing a fresh (slow) context build

javafs.title: Microservices, Resilience & Deployment
interviewFocus: Explain a multi-stage Dockerfile for a Spring app

resources.title: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud

questions.text: How do you make a call to another microservice resilient to that service being slow or down?
keyPoints: set an explicit timeout so a slow dependency can't hang your thread indefinitely
add retries with backoff for transient failures
add a circuit breaker (e.g., Resilience4j) to stop calling a failing service and fail fast, with a fallback response

questions.text: What's the benefit of a multi-stage Docker build for a Spring Boot app?
keyPoints: one stage builds/compiles the app (with the full JDK + build tool), a second stage copies only the built artifact into a minimal runtime image
this keeps the final image small and avoids shipping build tools/source code in production

questions.text: What are the typical stages of a CI/CD pipeline for a Spring Boot service?
keyPoints: build/compile -> run unit + integration tests -> static analysis/security scan -> build the container image -> deploy to staging -> (manual or automated) promote to production
the goal is to catch issues as early and cheaply as possible in the pipeline

questions.text: Synchronous REST calls vs an async message queue between microservices — when do you choose each?
keyPoints: sync REST: simple, immediate response needed, tighter coupling, caller blocks on the callee's availability
async messaging: decouples services, smooths load, survives temporary downstream outages, but adds eventual-consistency complexity

questions.text: What's the difference between a bulkhead and a circuit breaker, and why might you need both?
keyPoints: circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency entirely once its failure rate crosses a threshold
bulkhead limits how many concurrent calls/threads any ONE dependency can consume
they solve different problems — a bulkhead stops one slow dependency from starving calls to OTHER, healthy dependencies, which a circuit breaker alone doesn't prevent

questions.text: What's the difference between service discovery (like Eureka) and hardcoded service addresses?
keyPoints: service discovery lets instances register/deregister dynamically as they scale up/down or fail, with callers querying the registry at call time
hardcoded addresses break the moment an instance's address changes — common in cloud/container/auto-scaled environments

resources.title: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python

questions.text: Python is dynamically typed — what does that mean, and how does it differ from static typing?
keyPoints: a variable's type is determined at runtime by the object it references, not declared ahead of time
the same variable name can be rebound to a different type later
static typing (Java/C#) checks types at compile time instead

questions.text: What is the classic 'mutable default argument' bug in Python, and how do you avoid it?
keyPoints: a default argument like def f(items=[]) is evaluated ONCE at function definition time, not on every call
so mutations to that default list persist and leak across calls
fix: use None as the default and create the mutable object inside the function body

questions.text: Explain Python's LEGB rule for variable scope resolution.
keyPoints: Local -> Enclosing -> Global -> Built-in — the order Python searches when resolving a name
a local variable shadows an enclosing/global one of the same name; `global`/`nonlocal` keywords are needed to assign to an outer scope from inside a function

questions.text: What's the difference between == and is in Python?
keyPoints: == compares value/content equality (calls __eq__)
is compares object identity (same object in memory)
small integers and interned strings may be `is`-equal due to caching, which is an implementation detail you shouldn't rely on

questions.text: Python had no traditional switch statement before 3.10 — how did developers commonly emulate one, and what's the modern alternative?
keyPoints: commonly emulated with an if/elif chain, or a dictionary mapping keys to functions/values
Python 3.10+ added structural pattern matching via match/case as a real language-level alternative

questions.text: What's the difference between an f-string and .format() for string formatting, and why are f-strings generally preferred now?
keyPoints: f-strings (f"...") embed expressions directly inside the string literal, evaluated inline
.format() requires placeholder syntax with separate positional/keyword arguments
f-strings are more readable and also faster, since they're evaluated closer to bytecode level rather than via a method call

python.title: Data Structures & Collections
interviewFocus: Pick the right collection and justify it

resources.title: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python

questions.text: list vs tuple vs set vs dict — when do you reach for each?
keyPoints: list: ordered, mutable sequence — general-purpose collection
tuple: ordered, immutable — fixed records, safe to use as a dict key/hashable
set: unordered, unique elements, O(1) average membership test
dict: key-value mapping, O(1) average lookup by key

questions.text: What does list slicing like a[1:4:2] mean, and what does a[::-1] do?
keyPoints: a[start:stop:step] returns elements from index start up to (not including) stop, taking every `step`-th element
a[::-1] reverses the sequence — start and stop default to the full range, step -1 walks backward

questions.text: How would you rewrite a filter-and-transform for loop as a list comprehension, and when should you NOT use one?
keyPoints: a comprehension like [x*x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0] replaces a for loop that filters then appends
comprehensions are idiomatic and often faster for simple transforms/filters
nesting more than one or two conditions/loops hurts readability — a plain loop or a named function is clearer at that point

questions.text: What's the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy, and where does a shallow copy bite you?
keyPoints: a shallow copy (list(x), x.copy(), copy.copy()) creates a new outer container but reuses references to the same inner/nested objects
mutating a nested list/dict inside a shallow copy also mutates the original
copy.deepcopy() recursively copies nested objects to avoid this

questions.text: Why can a tuple be used as a dictionary key but a list cannot?
keyPoints: dict keys must be hashable
tuples are immutable and hashable, as long as everything inside them is also hashable
lists are mutable, so they're explicitly made unhashable — allowing them as keys would let a key's hash silently change after insertion, corrupting the dict

questions.text: What's a dict or set comprehension, and when would you reach for one over a list comprehension?
keyPoints: {k: v for ...} builds a dict, {x for ...} builds a set — the same comprehension syntax as a list but with different brackets
use a set comprehension when you need uniqueness or fast membership testing; a dict comprehension when transforming data into key-value pairs

resources.title: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python

questions.text: What do __init__ and self actually do in a Python class?
keyPoints: __init__ is the initializer, called automatically right after a new instance is created, to set up its initial state
self is the instance itself, passed automatically as the first parameter to instance methods — it's how a method accesses/modifies that specific object's attributes

questions.text: What is Method Resolution Order (MRO), and why does it matter with multiple inheritance?
keyPoints: MRO is the order Python searches base classes to resolve an attribute/method lookup, computed via the C3 linearization algorithm
it matters because with multiple inheritance, two parent classes could define the same method — MRO deterministically decides which one wins
you can inspect it with ClassName.__mro__ or ClassName.mro()

questions.text: What does implementing __eq__ and __hash__ let you do, and why must they be consistent?
keyPoints: __eq__ defines what == means for your objects; __hash__ defines their hash bucket for use as dict keys / set members
if two objects are equal (__eq__ True) but have different hashes, they'll silently break in sets/dicts — Python's contract requires equal objects to hash equally

questions.text: What does the @property decorator do, and why use it instead of plain getter/setter methods?
keyPoints: it lets a method be accessed like a plain attribute (obj.value instead of obj.get_value()) while still running code on access
it lets you start with plain public attributes and add validation/computed logic later without breaking the class's external API
common use: exposing a computed value (like a circle's area from its radius) as if it were a stored attribute

questions.text: What's the difference between a classmethod and a staticmethod in Python?
keyPoints: a classmethod receives the class itself as its first argument (cls) and can access/modify class-level state — commonly used as an alternative constructor
a staticmethod receives neither self nor cls — it's just a regular function namespaced inside the class for organizational purposes

questions.text: Python doesn't have true private attributes like Java — how do the single- and double-underscore conventions work?
keyPoints: a single leading underscore (_name) is a CONVENTION signaling 'internal use, don't touch' — it's not enforced by the language at all
a double leading underscore (__name) triggers name mangling (rewritten internally to _ClassName__name), making accidental access/override across subclasses harder, but still not truly private

resources.title: Automate the Boring Stuff with Python

questions.text: Explain how you'd write a decorator that times how long a function takes to run, mechanically.
keyPoints: a decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new (wrapper) function that adds behavior around the original call
the wrapper records a start time, calls the original function, records the end time, and returns the original result
functools.wraps is used on the wrapper to preserve the original function's name/docstring for introspection — a common thing junior candidates forget

questions.text: What's the difference between a generator and a normal function that returns a list, and why does it matter for memory?
keyPoints: a normal function computes and returns the entire list in memory at once
a generator (using yield) produces values lazily, one at a time, pausing its execution state between each — only one value needs to be in memory at a time
for very large or infinite sequences, a generator avoids loading everything into memory upfront

questions.text: Explain what try/except/else/finally each do, in order.
keyPoints: try: the code that might raise an exception
except: runs only if a matching exception was raised in the try block
else: runs only if the try block completed with NO exception raised
finally: always runs, whether or not an exception occurred — used for cleanup (closing files/connections)

questions.text: How does Python's `with` statement (a context manager) work, and why is it preferred over manual try/finally for resource cleanup?
keyPoints: the object's __enter__ method runs at the start of the block and __exit__ runs at the end — even if an exception occurred inside the block
a common example is opening a file: it's guaranteed to be closed when the block exits, even if an error was raised while reading it
it guarantees cleanup happens exactly once, in the right place, without the boilerplate and easy-to-forget-a-branch risk of manual try/finally

questions.text: When does it make sense to define a custom exception class in Python, and how do you typically define one?
keyPoints: when the failure represents a distinct, meaningful condition callers need to catch and handle specifically, not just a generic error
typically a simple subclass of Exception (or a more specific built-in), often needing nothing but `pass` as the body unless it carries extra fields

questions.text: What is a closure in Python, and how does it relate to decorators?
keyPoints: a closure is an inner function that 'remembers' variables from its enclosing scope even after the outer function has finished executing
decorators rely on closures — the wrapper function closes over the original function (and any decorator arguments) so it can call it later when the decorated function is actually invoked

python.title: Modules, Typing & Testing
interviewFocus: Why type hints don't enforce anything at runtime

questions.text: Do Python type hints get enforced at runtime? What are they actually for?
keyPoints: no — type hints are not checked or enforced when the code runs; Python remains fully dynamically typed at runtime
calling a hinted function with the 'wrong' type still runs without error — nothing raises a TypeError from the hints themselves
they're read by external static-analysis tools (mypy, IDEs, linters) to catch type mistakes before running the code, and they document intent for other developers

questions.text: What's the difference between a virtual environment (venv) and a requirements.txt file?
keyPoints: a venv is an isolated Python installation/directory holding a project's own interpreter and installed packages, separate from the system Python
requirements.txt is just a text list of package names/versions to install — it doesn't isolate anything by itself; `pip install -r requirements.txt` installs them, typically INTO an active venv

questions.text: What is a pytest fixture, and what problem does it solve?
keyPoints: a fixture is a reusable setup function (marked with @pytest.fixture) that provides test data, a DB connection, or a mock
pytest injects it automatically into any test function that names it as a parameter
it avoids duplicating the same setup/teardown code across many test functions

questions.text: How would you mock an external API call in a test so it doesn't make a real network request?
keyPoints: replace the function/method that performs the network call with a fake (a mock or monkeypatched function) that returns a canned response
patch it at the point where it's USED, not just where it's defined, so the test exercises your code's logic without depending on network availability or flakiness

questions.text: How does pytest's use of plain `assert` differ from a raw Python `assert` used for general debugging?
keyPoints: pytest rewrites plain assert statements in test files to give detailed failure output, showing the actual values on both sides of the comparison
outside pytest, Python's assert can be stripped entirely when running with the -O optimization flag, so it should never be relied on for real runtime validation

questions.text: What does `pip freeze > requirements.txt` capture, and what's a downside of using it directly for a shared project?
keyPoints: the EXACT versions of every package currently installed in the environment, including transitive dependencies

downside: it pins everything rigidly and can include packages only needed for local development, making the file harder to maintain than a curated list or a tool (Poetry/uv) that separates direct from transitive dependencies

python.title: Concurrency & Performance
interviewFocus: threading vs multiprocessing vs asyncio, correctly chosen
Where to actually profile before optimizing

resources.title: Speed Up Your Python Program With Concurrency

questions.text: What is the GIL, and what does it actually prevent?
keyPoints: the Global Interpreter Lock ensures only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time within a single process, even on a multi-core machine
it means Python threads do NOT give you true parallel CPU-bound execution — two threads can't run Python code simultaneously on two cores

questions.text: Given the GIL, when is Python threading still useful, and when do you need multiprocessing instead?
keyPoints: threading still helps for I/O-bound work (network calls, file/disk I/O) — the GIL is released while waiting on I/O, so threads overlap that waiting time
multiprocessing runs separate Python processes, each with its own GIL/interpreter, giving true parallelism for CPU-bound work (heavy computation)
rule of thumb: I/O-bound -> threading (or asyncio); CPU-bound -> multiprocessing

questions.text: What problem does asyncio solve, and how is it different from threading?
keyPoints: asyncio runs many I/O-bound tasks concurrently on a SINGLE thread using cooperative multitasking — a task voluntarily yields control (at an `await`) while waiting on I/O instead of blocking

```python
import asyncio

async def fetch(url):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # simulates a non-blocking I/O wait
    return f"data from {url}"

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(fetch("a"), fetch("b"))
```
unlike threading, there's no preemptive context-switching or thread-safety overhead — but a single long-running CPU-bound `await`-free call will block the whole event loop

questions.text: Before optimizing slow Python code, what should you do first, and why?
keyPoints: profile it (e.g., with cProfile or a line profiler) to find where time is ACTUALLY being spent, rather than guessing
most code has one or two real bottlenecks — optimizing code that isn't actually slow wastes effort and adds complexity for no measurable benefit

questions.text: What's the overhead cost of multiprocessing compared to threading, and why does it matter for choosing between them?
keyPoints: each process has its own separate memory space, so data must be serialized (pickled) and copied between processes rather than shared directly
multiprocessing pays a real startup and inter-process-communication cost, so it's worth it only when the CPU-bound work is substantial enough to outweigh that overhead

questions.text: Can you mix asyncio with blocking (synchronous) code, and what happens if you do it carelessly?
keyPoints: calling a blocking function directly inside an async function freezes the ENTIRE event loop for its duration
asyncio is single-threaded cooperative multitasking, so one blocking call stalls every other coroutine waiting on that loop
the fix is running blocking calls in a thread pool executor (loop.run_in_executor) so they don't block the rest of the event loop

java.title: OOP & Language Fundamentals
objectives: The four pillars of OOP in Java
interviewFocus: Explain each OOP pillar with a Java example
Why overriding equals() requires overriding hashCode()

resources.title: Why String is immutable in Java

questions.text: What are the four pillars of OOP, and how does Java express each one?
keyPoints: encapsulation: private fields + public getters/setters hide internal state
inheritance: extends/implements lets a class reuse and specialize another type's behavior
polymorphism: a subclass reference used through its parent type, with the actual overridden method resolved at runtime (dynamic dispatch)
abstraction: abstract classes and interfaces expose a contract without committing to implementation details

questions.text: Why is String immutable in Java, and what is the string constant pool?
keyPoints: immutability makes String safe to share across threads without synchronization, safe as a HashMap key (hashCode can be cached), and safe to intern
the string pool is a special memory area where literal strings are cached and reused — two identical literals point to the same object, saving memory
string concatenation with + creates new objects, which is why StringBuilder is preferred in loops

questions.text: What is the contract between equals() and hashCode(), and what breaks if you violate it?
keyPoints: if two objects are equal per equals(), they MUST return the same hashCode()
the reverse isn't required — unequal objects may share a hash code (a collision), just less efficiently
violating this contract breaks hash-based collections like HashMap/HashSet: an object can be 'lost' (inserted under one bucket, looked up in another) even though equals() says it should be found

questions.text: == vs .equals() — what's the difference for objects, and why does it matter for String specifically?
keyPoints: == compares references (are these the same object in memory) for any object type
.equals() compares logical/value equality, as defined by the class's own override
for Strings, two different literals may or may not be == depending on interning, so relying on == for string comparison is a common, subtle bug — always use .equals()

questions.text: What are Java's access modifiers, and what's the difference between protected and package-private (no modifier)?
keyPoints: public: accessible everywhere; private: same class only
package-private (default, no modifier): accessible within the same package only
protected: package-private access PLUS accessible to subclasses even in a different package — broader than package-private specifically for inheritance

questions.text: What does toString() do by default, and why do you almost always override it?
keyPoints: Object's default toString() returns the class name plus a hex representation of the hash code — not useful for debugging
overriding it to print meaningful field values makes logging, debugging, and println output actually readable

java.title: Collections Framework Deep Dive
interviewFocus: Pick the right List/Set/Map for a scenario and justify it
Comparable vs Comparator, with when to use each

questions.text: HashSet vs TreeSet vs LinkedHashSet — how do they differ and when would you pick each?
keyPoints: HashSet: no ordering guarantee, O(1) average add/contains, backed by a HashMap
LinkedHashSet: preserves insertion order, small extra overhead over HashSet
TreeSet: keeps elements sorted (natural order or a Comparator), O(log n) operations, backed by a red-black tree
pick HashSet by default for pure uniqueness, LinkedHashSet when insertion order matters for iteration/output, TreeSet when you need sorted iteration

questions.text: What causes a ConcurrentModificationException, and how do you safely remove elements while iterating?
keyPoints: structurally modifying a collection (add/remove) directly while iterating over it with a for-each loop invalidates the iterator's internal modCount check
fix by using the Iterator's own remove() method, or a CopyOnWriteArrayList/ConcurrentHashMap for concurrent scenarios, or collecting items to remove and removing them after the loop

questions.text: Comparable vs Comparator — what's the difference and when do you use each?
keyPoints: Comparable: implemented BY the class itself (compareTo), defines that type's single 'natural' ordering
Comparator: a separate strategy object (compare), lets you define multiple different orderings without touching the class, and can be composed (thenComparing)
use Comparable when there's one obvious default ordering; use Comparator for ad-hoc or multiple orderings, especially for classes you don't own

questions.text: Why is it usually a bad idea to use a mutable object as a HashMap key?
keyPoints: the key's hashCode is used to place it in a bucket at insertion time
if the key object is later mutated in a way that changes its hashCode/equals result, the map can no longer find it in the correct bucket — the entry becomes effectively lost
prefer immutable keys (String, wrapper types, records, or objects deliberately designed to be immutable)

questions.text: What's the difference between a fail-fast and a fail-safe iterator, with an example of each?
keyPoints: fail-fast (ArrayList, HashMap): throws ConcurrentModificationException if the collection is structurally modified during iteration, detected via a modCount check
fail-safe (CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap): iterates over a snapshot or otherwise tolerates concurrent modification without throwing

questions.text: What ordering guarantee does a PriorityQueue provide, and what's a common interview use for it?
keyPoints: PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default (or ordered by a supplied Comparator) — it only guarantees the smallest/highest-priority element is at the head, NOT that the whole queue is sorted
common uses: 'k largest/smallest elements', Dijkstra's algorithm, merging k sorted lists

java.title: Exceptions, I/O & NIO
interviewFocus: Checked vs unchecked, with a design rationale
When to write a custom exception

questions.text: Checked vs unchecked exceptions — what's the difference, and how should you decide which to use for a new exception type?
keyPoints: checked exceptions (extend Exception, not RuntimeException) must be declared or caught — the compiler enforces handling
unchecked exceptions (extend RuntimeException) don't require declaration — used for programming errors or conditions the caller usually can't recover from
modern guidance leans toward unchecked for most application exceptions, reserving checked exceptions for conditions a caller is genuinely expected to recover from

questions.text: What does try-with-resources do, and what interface must a resource implement to use it?
keyPoints: the resource must implement AutoCloseable (or Closeable)
the compiler automatically generates a finally block that calls close() on the resource(s), even if an exception is thrown, in reverse order of declaration
this eliminates the boilerplate and bug-risk of manually writing finally { resource.close(); }

questions.text: When does it make sense to create a custom exception class instead of reusing a built-in one?
keyPoints: when the exception represents a distinct, meaningful business/domain condition callers need to catch and handle specifically (e.g., InsufficientFundsException)
custom exceptions can carry extra context (fields) relevant to that failure
avoid overusing custom exceptions for cases a standard exception (IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException) already covers clearly

questions.text: What's the difference between the older java.io streams and java.nio, at a conceptual level?
keyPoints: java.io is stream-based and blocking — you read/write sequentially and the thread blocks while waiting
java.nio adds buffer/channel-based I/O and (via NIO.2 in java.nio.file) a much better file API (Path, Files), plus non-blocking/selector-based I/O for scalable network servers
for typical file operations today, java.nio.file's Files/Path API is preferred over the legacy File class

questions.text: What happens if BOTH the try block AND the resource's close() throw an exception in try-with-resources?
keyPoints: the try block's ORIGINAL exception propagates as the primary one
the close() exception is attached to it as a 'suppressed exception' (retrievable via getSuppressed()), not silently lost and not replacing the original

questions.text: What's the difference between Error and Exception in terms of what a well-behaved application should do with each?
keyPoints: Exception represents conditions an application is expected to anticipate and handle
Error (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) signals the JVM itself is in serious trouble
catching/'handling' an Error is rarely correct — the right response is usually to let the process fail and be restarted/monitored

java.title: Multithreading & Concurrency
objectives: Locks, synchronized & the Java Memory Model
interviewFocus: Explain the Java Memory Model & volatile
Design a thread pool for a workload

questions.text: What does the volatile keyword guarantee, and what does it NOT guarantee?
keyPoints: volatile guarantees visibility — a write to a volatile field is immediately visible to all threads (no stale cached value), and it prevents certain reorderings
it does NOT guarantee atomicity for compound operations like i++ — a read-modify-write on a volatile field can still race
use volatile for simple flags/single-value visibility; use synchronized/atomic classes/locks when you need atomicity too

questions.text: Why prefer an ExecutorService/thread pool over creating raw new Thread() instances?
keyPoints: creating a new OS thread per task is expensive (memory + context-switch overhead) and gives you no control over concurrency limits
a thread pool reuses a bounded set of worker threads, queues excess work, and gives you lifecycle control (shutdown, awaitTermination) and back-pressure
choosing pool size/type (fixed, cached, work-stealing/ForkJoinPool) should match whether the workload is CPU-bound or I/O-bound

questions.text: What is a race condition, and name two different ways to prevent one on a shared counter.
keyPoints: a race condition happens when multiple threads read-modify-write shared state without coordination, so the final result depends on unlucky interleaving
option 1: synchronize the critical section (synchronized block/method or a Lock) so only one thread mutates it at a time
option 2: use an atomic class (AtomicInteger/AtomicLong) which performs the update via a lock-free CAS (compare-and-swap) loop

questions.text: What does CompletableFuture.thenApply vs thenCompose do differently, and why does that distinction matter?
keyPoints: thenApply transforms the result with a plain function (T -> U) — use it when the next step is synchronous
thenCompose chains to another CompletableFuture-returning function (T -> CompletableFuture<U>) and flattens the result — use it when the next step is itself async, to avoid nested futures
using thenApply where thenCompose is needed produces a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<U>>, which is almost never what you want

questions.text: What are the states in a Java thread's lifecycle, and what causes a thread to move from RUNNABLE to WAITING?
keyPoints: NEW -> RUNNABLE -> (BLOCKED / WAITING / TIMED_WAITING) -> TERMINATED
a thread moves to WAITING when it calls a blocking method without a timeout — e.g. Object.wait() or Thread.join() — until another thread notifies it or completes

questions.text: What's a deadlock, and what's the standard practical technique to prevent one?
keyPoints: a cycle of threads each waiting for a resource held by another, so none can proceed
the standard fix: always acquire locks in the same, globally consistent order across every thread, eliminating the circular-wait condition a deadlock requires

java.title: JVM Internals & Memory Management
objectives: Reading a stack trace & basic JVM tuning
interviewFocus: Draw the JVM memory layout from memory
Compare G1, Parallel and ZGC at a high level

questions.text: What are the main JVM runtime memory areas, and what lives in each?
keyPoints: heap: all objects and arrays live here, shared across threads, divided into young (eden + survivor) and old generation
stack: one per thread, holds method call frames — local variables and partial results; a runaway recursion causes a StackOverflowError here
metaspace (replaced PermGen since Java 8): class metadata, native memory rather than heap
an OutOfMemoryError can come from any of these being exhausted, and the specific message tells you which

questions.text: At a high level, how does a generational garbage collector (like G1) decide what to collect, and why generational?
keyPoints: the 'weak generational hypothesis' observes most objects die young — so the young generation is collected frequently and cheaply (minor GC), promoting survivors to the old generation
the old generation is collected less often since most long-lived objects genuinely stay alive, making full/mixed collections rarer and more expensive
G1 further divides the heap into regions and prioritizes collecting the regions with the most garbage first ('garbage first')

questions.text: What's the difference between ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError?
keyPoints: ClassNotFoundException: a checked exception thrown when code explicitly tries to load a class by name (e.g., Class.forName) and it isn't found on the classpath

NoClassDefFoundError: an Error thrown when a class WAS available at compile time but is missing at runtime when the JVM tries to link/use it — often a packaging/classpath mismatch between build and deploy

questions.text: What's the difference between a memory leak in Java and one in a language like C, given Java has garbage collection?
keyPoints: Java can still leak memory — not by forgetting to free it, but by keeping unintended references alive (e.g., a growing static collection, unclosed listeners, ThreadLocal not cleared) so the GC can never reclaim those objects
the fix is finding and breaking the unwanted reference chain (often via a heap dump analysis tool), not manual memory management

questions.text: What's the parent-delegation model for Java class loaders, and why does it matter?
keyPoints: a class loader asks its PARENT to try loading a class first (bootstrap -> platform -> application) before attempting itself
this is why you can't accidentally shadow a core class like java.lang.String with your own class of the same name

questions.text: What JVM flags control the initial and maximum heap size, and what's a common production tuning practice around them?
keyPoints: -Xms sets the INITIAL heap size, -Xmx sets the MAXIMUM heap size
a common production practice is setting them to the SAME value, so the heap is allocated up front instead of paying the pause cost of growing gradually under load

java.title: Modern Java (8-21) Features
interviewFocus: Explain why Optional isn't meant for fields/parameters
Records vs classes, and what virtual threads change

questions.text: What's the difference between an intermediate and a terminal Stream operation, and why does that matter for performance?
keyPoints: intermediate operations (map, filter, sorted) are LAZY — they just build up a pipeline description and don't run anything yet
a terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce) triggers actual evaluation of the whole pipeline, element by element
laziness lets the JVM avoid unnecessary work, e.g., short-circuiting with findFirst() without processing the whole source

questions.text: Why is Optional generally discouraged as a field type or method parameter?
keyPoints: Optional was designed specifically as a RETURN type to signal 'this method may not have a result', to be checked by the caller instead of returning null
using it as a field adds serialization/boilerplate overhead with no real benefit over just allowing the field to be null (and documenting that)
using it as a parameter forces every caller to wrap a value in Optional.of just to call the method — overloading or a sensible default is usually cleaner

questions.text: What problem do Java records solve, and what do you get 'for free' by declaring one?
keyPoints: records eliminate the boilerplate of a plain immutable data-carrier class

declaring record Point(int x, int y) {} automatically generates a canonical constructor, private final fields, accessor methods (x(), y()), and correct equals/hashCode/toString based on the components
records are implicitly final and can't extend another class (though they can implement interfaces), reinforcing that they're meant to model simple immutable data

questions.text: What are virtual threads (Java 21), and what kind of workload benefits most from them?
keyPoints: virtual threads are lightweight threads managed by the JVM rather than mapped 1:1 to an OS thread — you can create millions of them cheaply

they benefit I/O-bound workloads most: a virtual thread that blocks on I/O (e.g., a DB call, an HTTP call) is 'unmounted' from its carrier OS thread, freeing that OS thread to run other virtual threads, instead of the OS thread sitting idle
they don't speed up CPU-bound work — for that, the number of CPU cores is still the real limit

questions.text: What are sealed classes/interfaces, and what benefit do they provide with pattern matching in a switch?
keyPoints: sealed restricts exactly which classes/interfaces are allowed to extend/implement a type, declared via a permits clause
combined with pattern matching for switch, the compiler can verify EXHAUSTIVENESS — forgetting to handle a newly-added permitted subtype becomes a compile error instead of a silent runtime gap
