questions.text: What does pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16+) eliminate compared to the old style?
keyPoints: the old style requires an instanceof check followed by a separate, redundant explicit cast
pattern matching binds a pattern variable, already narrowed to the checked type, directly in the instanceof condition — removing the cast and a whole class of cast-mismatch bugs

spring.title: IoC Container & Dependency Injection
objectives: Constructor vs setter vs field injection
Java config vs XML vs component scanning
interviewFocus: Justify constructor injection as the default
Name all standard bean scopes and when each applies

questions.text: What's the difference between Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection?
keyPoints: IoC is the broader principle: control over object creation/wiring is inverted from the code itself to a container/framework
DI is ONE specific technique for achieving IoC — the container supplies (injects) a component's dependencies rather than the component looking them up or creating them itself
other IoC techniques exist (e.g., service locator) but DI is what Spring is built around

questions.text: Why does Spring documentation recommend constructor injection as the default choice?
keyPoints: it makes required dependencies explicit and allows fields to be declared final (immutable after construction)
it fails fast at application startup if a required dependency is missing, rather than surfacing a NullPointerException later at runtime
it makes unit testing trivial — you just call the constructor with mocks, no reflection or Spring context needed
field injection, by contrast, hides dependencies, allows constructing an incomplete object, and requires a DI framework (or reflection) even in tests

questions.text: List Spring's standard bean scopes and when you'd use each.
keyPoints: singleton (default): one instance per Spring container — the right choice for stateless, shared services
prototype: a new instance every time the bean is requested — for stateful or non-thread-safe objects
request/session/application: web-aware scopes tied to an HTTP request, session, or ServletContext respectively — used for web-tier beans that must not be shared across users

questions.text: What's the difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository and @Controller, given they all register a bean the same way?
keyPoints: functionally, all four are stereotypes of @Component and register a bean identically via component scanning

the more specific ones add semantic meaning for readability AND extra framework behavior — @Repository enables Spring's exception translation (wrapping JDBC/JPA exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy)
using the right stereotype documents the layer a class belongs to, which also helps AOP pointcuts that target a layer by annotation

questions.text: What's the difference between Java-based configuration (@Configuration/@Bean) and XML-based configuration in Spring?
keyPoints: Java config is type-safe and refactorable, and lets you write real conditional/programmatic logic when constructing a bean
XML config lives entirely outside the code with no compile-time checking, but fully separates configuration from code
Java config is the modern default recommendation; XML is mostly seen in older/legacy Spring codebases

questions.text: What's the difference between BeanFactory and ApplicationContext?
keyPoints: BeanFactory is the root, minimal IoC container interface — lazy bean instantiation, few features

ApplicationContext extends BeanFactory and adds enterprise features used by virtually every real app: eager singleton instantiation at startup (so config errors surface immediately), event publishing, and i18n support
in practice almost nobody works with raw BeanFactory directly

spring.title: AOP & Cross-Cutting Concerns
interviewFocus: Explain a cross-cutting concern with an example
JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB proxy
Why calling a @Transactional method from within the same class doesn't work

questions.text: What problem does AOP solve, and what's a concrete example of a cross-cutting concern in a typical Spring app?
keyPoints: cross-cutting concerns are behaviors needed across many unrelated classes (logging, security checks, transaction management, caching) that would otherwise be duplicated in every method
AOP lets you define that behavior ONCE as an aspect and apply it declaratively wherever a pointcut expression matches, keeping business logic classes focused on their actual responsibility
example: @Transactional itself is implemented as AOP advice wrapping a method call in a transaction

questions.text: How does Spring implement AOP under the hood — JDK dynamic proxies vs CGLIB?
keyPoints: Spring AOP is proxy-based: it wraps your bean in a proxy object that intercepts method calls
JDK dynamic proxies are used when the target class implements at least one interface — the proxy implements the same interface(s)
CGLIB proxies (subclassing) are used when there's no interface — the proxy subclasses the target class at runtime, which is why AOP doesn't work on final classes/methods

questions.text: Why does calling a @Transactional-annotated method from another method in the SAME class not actually start a transaction?
keyPoints: Spring AOP proxies work by intercepting calls made TO the proxy from outside — an internal self-invocation (this.method()) bypasses the proxy entirely and calls the real method directly
fix by injecting a self-reference/using AopContext.currentProxy(), or better, moving the @Transactional method into a separate collaborating bean that gets called through its own proxy

questions.text: What's the difference between @Before, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @After and @Around advice?
keyPoints: @Before runs before the method; @AfterReturning runs after a successful return; @AfterThrowing runs only if an exception propagates out; @After runs regardless (like finally)

@Around is the most powerful: it wraps the whole invocation, receives a ProceedingJoinPoint, and can choose whether/when to call proceed(), inspect/modify the return value, or short-circuit the call entirely

questions.text: What's a pointcut expression, and describe one that matches all public methods in a service package.
keyPoints: a pointcut defines WHICH join points (method executions) an aspect's advice applies to, matched by pattern against modifiers/return type/package/class/method/parameters
example: execution(public * com.app.service..*.*(..)) — any public method, any return type, in that package or sub-packages, any class, any method name, any parameters

questions.text: Can Spring AOP apply advice to an object created directly with `new`, outside the Spring container?
keyPoints: no — Spring AOP only works on beans the container itself creates and wraps in a proxy AT CREATION TIME
an object created with `new` bypasses the container entirely, so no proxy is ever created and no advice applies, regardless of matching pointcuts

spring.title: Spring MVC & Web Layer
interviewFocus: Trace a request from DispatcherServlet to the response

questions.text: Walk through what happens to an HTTP request from the moment it hits DispatcherServlet.
keyPoints: DispatcherServlet (the front controller) receives the request and asks a HandlerMapping which controller method should handle it
a HandlerAdapter invokes that controller method, resolving method arguments (path variables, request body, etc.) along the way
the controller returns a value; if it's a ResponseEntity or an @ResponseBody-annotated result, an HttpMessageConverter serializes it (e.g., to JSON) directly to the response
if it's a view name instead, a ViewResolver locates and renders the corresponding view

questions.text: How do you validate an incoming request body, and what happens if validation fails?
keyPoints: annotate the parameter with @Valid (or @Validated) and the DTO fields with Bean Validation annotations (@NotNull, @Size, @Email, etc.)
by default, a failed validation throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, which Spring Boot turns into a 400 response automatically
alternatively, add a BindingResult parameter right after the @Valid argument to inspect errors yourself instead of letting the exception propagate

questions.text: @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler vs a try/catch in each controller method — why prefer the former?
keyPoints: @ControllerAdvice centralizes exception-to-response mapping in ONE place, applied globally across all (or a targeted subset of) controllers
it keeps controller methods focused on the happy path instead of repeating the same error-formatting logic everywhere
it produces consistent error response shapes across the whole API, which API consumers can rely on

questions.text: What's the difference between @RequestParam, @PathVariable and @RequestBody?
keyPoints: @RequestParam binds a query string parameter (?name=value) or form field
@PathVariable binds a segment of the URI path itself (e.g., /users/{id})
@RequestBody deserializes the entire HTTP request body (typically JSON) into a Java object using an HttpMessageConverter

questions.text: What's content negotiation in Spring MVC, and how does the framework decide whether to return JSON or XML from the same endpoint?
keyPoints: content negotiation picks the response representation format based on what the client asked for, primarily the Accept header
Spring's ContentNegotiationManager inspects these signals and picks a registered HttpMessageConverter capable of producing that format

questions.text: What's the difference between @Controller and @RestController?
keyPoints: @Controller returns a view name by default, to be resolved and rendered as HTML (e.g. via Thymeleaf) — not sent as the raw response body
@RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody, so every method's return value is serialized directly into the response body — the standard choice for a JSON REST API

questions.text: What's the difference between declarative and programmatic transaction management in Spring, and which does Spring generally recommend?
keyPoints: declarative: annotate a method with @Transactional and let an AOP proxy start/commit/rollback the transaction around it — no transaction code in your business logic
programmatic: manually use TransactionTemplate or PlatformTransactionManager to control transaction boundaries in code

Spring recommends declarative for the vast majority of cases — it's less error-prone and keeps transaction concerns out of business logic; programmatic is reserved for cases needing fine-grained control within a single method

questions.text: Explain REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW, and NESTED propagation, and how they differ in rollback behavior.
keyPoints: REQUIRED (default): joins the caller's existing transaction if one exists, else starts a new one — a rollback anywhere in that shared transaction rolls back everything
REQUIRES_NEW: always suspends any existing transaction and starts a fully independent new one — the outer transaction's rollback does NOT undo what the inner one already committed

NESTED: uses a savepoint within the SAME physical transaction — a rollback in the nested part can be contained (rolled back to the savepoint) without necessarily rolling back the whole outer transaction, but it's still tied to the outer transaction's ultimate commit/rollback

questions.text: What is Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy, and why does it matter that it's unchecked?
keyPoints: Spring translates low-level, technology-specific exceptions (SQLException, Hibernate exceptions, etc.) into a consistent, technology-agnostic DataAccessException hierarchy

being unchecked (a RuntimeException subtype) means callers aren't forced to catch/declare it everywhere, and the abstraction lets you swap the underlying persistence technology without changing every catch clause up the call stack
this translation is what @Repository's stereotype behavior enables via a BeanPostProcessor

questions.text: When would you reach for JdbcTemplate instead of an ORM like Hibernate/Spring Data JPA?
keyPoints: when you need tight control over the exact SQL executed (complex reporting queries, bulk operations, performance-critical paths where ORM-generated SQL is suboptimal)
JdbcTemplate removes JDBC boilerplate (connection/statement/resultset handling, resource closing) while still letting you write raw SQL
for typical CRUD-heavy domain-object persistence, an ORM/Spring Data JPA is usually more productive; JdbcTemplate is the pragmatic escape hatch

questions.text: What are the standard transaction isolation levels, and what's Spring's default if you don't specify one?
keyPoints: READ_UNCOMMITTED, READ_COMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ, SERIALIZABLE, in increasing strictness
Spring's default is ISOLATION_DEFAULT, which delegates to whatever the underlying database's own default isolation level is (commonly READ_COMMITTED for most relational databases)

questions.text: What does RowMapper do in JdbcTemplate?
keyPoints: converts ONE row of a JDBC ResultSet into a domain object
JdbcTemplate calls it once per row and collects the results into a list, handling ResultSet iteration and resource cleanup for you

spring.title: Spring Testing
objectives: Mocking beans in a Spring test
interviewFocus: MockMvc vs a real running server for a controller test

questions.text: Why does Spring's TestContextFramework cache the ApplicationContext between test classes, and what can accidentally break that caching?
keyPoints: starting a full Spring context is expensive; caching it (keyed by its configuration) lets many test classes share the SAME context instead of rebuilding it per class, dramatically speeding up a test suite

anything that changes the effective configuration key breaks the cache and forces a rebuild — e.g., different @ActiveProfiles, different @MockBean sets, or different context configuration classes between test classes
minimizing unique context configurations across a test suite is a real, practical performance technique

questions.text: What does MockMvc give you that a full @SpringBootTest with a real embedded server doesn't, for testing a controller?
keyPoints: MockMvc simulates HTTP requests/responses against the DispatcherServlet WITHOUT starting an actual network server/port — faster, and still exercises the real MVC request-handling pipeline (argument resolution, validation, exception handling, serialization)

a full embedded-server test (@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment=RANDOM_PORT) + a real HTTP client) is slower but verifies actual network behavior end-to-end, useful for a smaller number of true integration tests

questions.text: What's the difference between a test slice like @WebMvcTest and the full @SpringBootTest?
keyPoints: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers, filters, MVC infra) and auto-configures MockMvc, leaving service/repository beans unloaded — you supply mocks (e.g., @MockBean) for them
@SpringBootTest loads the entire application context, which is thorough but much slower — appropriate for true end-to-end integration tests, not for testing one controller in isolation

questions.text: What's the difference between @MockBean and a manually created Mockito mock inside a Spring test?
keyPoints: @MockBean replaces the real bean of that type INSIDE the Spring application context, so any other bean autowiring that dependency transparently gets the mock
a plain Mockito.mock() is just a local object you wire yourself and never touches the Spring context — much faster for a pure unit test that doesn't need Spring running at all

questions.text: What does @DataJpaTest do differently from @SpringBootTest when testing a repository?
keyPoints: @DataJpaTest loads only the JPA-related slice (repositories, entity scanning, a test database) and by default rolls back each test's transaction automatically
@SpringBootTest loads the entire application, unnecessary overhead just to verify a query method returns the right rows

questions.text: Why might introducing a new @MockBean in one test class slow down the ENTIRE test suite, even though the mock itself is fast?
keyPoints: @MockBean changes the effective ApplicationContext configuration for that class, and that configuration is part of Spring's test-context cache key
a new, previously-unseen combination of mocks forces a fresh (uncached) context build instead of reusing one — and many test classes each doing this uniquely defeats caching across the whole suite

springboot.title: Auto-Configuration & Starters
interviewFocus: Property override precedence across profiles/env vars/args

questions.text: What three annotations does @SpringBootApplication compose, and what does each contribute?
keyPoints: @SpringBootConfiguration: marks the class as a source of bean definitions (a specialization of @Configuration)
@EnableAutoConfiguration: triggers Spring Boot's auto-configuration mechanism, which conditionally registers beans based on the classpath and existing configuration
@ComponentScan: scans the current package (and sub-packages) for @Component-annotated classes to register as beans

questions.text: How does a single Spring Boot 'starter' dependency end up auto-configuring an entire subsystem, like spring-boot-starter-data-jpa?
keyPoints: the starter is really just a curated set of transitive dependencies (Hibernate, Spring Data JPA, a JDBC driver, etc.) with compatible versions — it doesn't itself contain framework code

adding those jars to the classpath is what auto-configuration classes react to via @ConditionalOnClass — e.g., seeing Hibernate + a DataSource on the classpath triggers JPA-related beans to auto-configure
you can always override any auto-configured bean by defining your own bean of that type — @ConditionalOnMissingBean means your explicit bean wins

questions.text: What's the property override precedence in Spring Boot when the same property is set in application.yml, an environment variable, and a command-line argument?
keyPoints: command-line arguments win over almost everything else
environment variables and JVM system properties come next, ahead of the packaged application.properties/yml
profile-specific files (application-{profile}.yml) override the base application.yml for properties they redefine
understanding this order matters for debugging 'why isn't my config taking effect' issues in different environments

questions.text: How would you disable a specific auto-configuration class you don't want (e.g., the default DataSource auto-config)?
keyPoints: use @SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class) or the spring.autoconfigure.exclude property
this is common when you want to configure that concern manually, or when a starter on the classpath brings auto-configuration you don't actually want active

questions.text: How are Spring Boot's many auto-configuration classes ordered against each other, and why does that ordering matter?
keyPoints: auto-configuration classes carry @AutoConfigureAfter/@AutoConfigureBefore/@AutoConfigureOrder metadata that controls the sequence they're evaluated in

ordering matters because a later auto-configuration's conditions (like @ConditionalOnMissingBean) often depend on beans an earlier one already registered — e.g., a web auto-configuration might need to run after the base DataSource auto-configuration is in place
spring.factories / AutoConfiguration.imports lists the candidate classes, but it's this relative ordering metadata (not file order) that determines evaluation sequence

questions.text: You have application.yml plus application-dev.yml and application-prod.yml. How does Spring Boot decide which profile-specific properties apply, and what happens on a conflict?
keyPoints: the active profile(s) are selected via spring.profiles.active (set as an env var, JVM arg, or in the base file itself)
Spring Boot loads the base application.yml first, then layers the matching profile-specific file on top — properties in the profile-specific file override the same key in the base file
if multiple profiles are active at once, later-declared profiles in spring.profiles.active take precedence over earlier ones for the same key

springboot.title: Spring Data JPA in Boot
interviewFocus: Derive a query method from its name
Diagnose and fix an N+1 query
Explain why migrations belong in version control

questions.text: How does Spring Data JPA generate a working query just from a method name like findByLastNameAndActiveTrue?
keyPoints: Spring Data parses the method name against a defined grammar (By, And, Or, property names, keywords like GreaterThan/OrderBy) and builds the equivalent JPQL query at startup, without you writing any SQL/JPQL
for anything the naming convention can't express cleanly, you fall back to @Query with JPQL or native SQL

questions.text: What is the N+1 query problem in a Spring Data JPA repository, concretely, and how do you fix it?
keyPoints: calling findAll() on an entity that has a lazy @OneToMany, then accessing that collection for each of the N results triggers 1 query for the list plus N additional queries — one per entity
fix with a JOIN FETCH in a custom @Query, an @EntityGraph on the repository method, or batch fetching (hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size) to collapse the N extra queries into far fewer

questions.text: Where should @Transactional boundaries typically live in a Spring Boot app — the controller, service, or repository layer — and why?
keyPoints: the service layer — it represents a meaningful unit of business work that may span multiple repository calls that must succeed or fail together

controllers shouldn't hold transactions open across HTTP-layer concerns (like serialization); repositories are too fine-grained and would create a separate transaction per data-access call, defeating the purpose

questions.text: Why use a migration tool like Flyway or Liquibase instead of letting Hibernate auto-generate/update the schema (ddl-auto=update)?
keyPoints: ddl-auto=update is convenient for local dev but unsafe in production — it can silently make destructive or unexpected changes, and there's no audit trail or rollback
Flyway/Liquibase store versioned, ordered migration scripts that are applied deterministically and consistently across every environment, forming a reviewable history of every schema change
the standard practice is ddl-auto=validate (or none) in production, with real migrations owning schema evolution

questions.text: When would a derived query method name stop being the right tool, and what do you reach for instead?
keyPoints: once the condition logic gets complex (many ANDs/ORs, joins across relationships, aggregations, or dynamic/optional filters), the method name becomes unreadable or simply can't express it

@Query with JPQL (or native SQL) for fixed but complex queries, or the Specification/Criteria API for queries whose filters are built dynamically at runtime based on which parameters were actually supplied
readability and maintainability, not just capability, is often the real deciding factor for switching away from derived names

questions.text: What does @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW) do differently from the default REQUIRED, and give a real scenario where you'd need it?
keyPoints: REQUIRED (default) joins the caller's existing transaction if one is active, or starts a new one if not — so if the outer transaction rolls back, this method's work rolls back with it
REQUIRES_NEW always suspends any existing transaction and starts a completely independent one that commits or rolls back on its own

a real scenario: writing an audit log entry that must persist even if the surrounding business operation later fails and rolls back — running it in REQUIRES_NEW means the audit record survives regardless of the outer transaction's fate

springboot.title: REST APIs, Validation & Error Handling
interviewFocus: Design clean, RESTful resource URIs and status codes

resources.title: REST APIs with Spring Boot masterclass

questions.text: What makes a REST API 'RESTful' rather than just an HTTP API — name a few concrete practices.
keyPoints: resource-oriented URIs (nouns, not verbs: /orders/{id}, not /getOrder)
correct use of HTTP methods (GET for reads, POST to create, PUT/PATCH to update, DELETE to remove) and status codes (201 Created with a Location header, 404, 409, etc.)
statelessness — each request contains everything needed to process it, no server-side session state between requests
HATEOAS (hypermedia links) is the more purist/advanced criterion, though many production APIs skip it pragmatically

questions.text: How do you return a consistent, structured error body across every endpoint in a Spring Boot API?
keyPoints: a single @RestControllerAdvice class with @ExceptionHandler methods per exception type (or exception hierarchy), each returning a consistent error DTO (status, message, timestamp, maybe a field-level validation error list)
Spring Boot 3+ also supports RFC 7807 'Problem Details' (ProblemDetail) out of the box as a standardized error response format

questions.text: How do you validate a request DTO's fields and return a useful 400 response listing exactly what's wrong?
keyPoints: annotate the DTO fields with Bean Validation (@NotBlank, @Size, @Min, @Email, etc.) and the controller parameter with @Valid

catch MethodArgumentNotValidException in an @ExceptionHandler and map its BindingResult/FieldErrors into a response listing each invalid field and its specific message, rather than a single generic 400

questions.text: What does OpenAPI/Swagger give you in a Spring Boot project, and how is it typically generated?
keyPoints: a machine-readable specification of your API's endpoints, request/response shapes, and status codes — enabling interactive docs (Swagger UI) and client-code generation
springdoc-openapi generates it automatically from your controllers/DTOs and annotations at runtime, rather than you hand-writing a YAML/JSON spec

questions.text: How would you design pagination and sorting for a GET /orders endpoint that could return millions of rows?
keyPoints: accept page/size (or a cursor) and sort query parameters rather than always returning the full collection
Spring Data's Pageable/Page support maps these directly onto a repository method and returns metadata (total elements, total pages, current page) alongside the content

offset-based paging (page/size) degrades on very large datasets — cursor/keyset pagination (using the last seen ID or sort key) avoids the cost of skipping millions of rows and stays stable when rows are inserted between requests

questions.text: How do you version a REST API in Spring Boot without breaking existing clients when you need to change a resource's shape?
keyPoints: common approaches: a URI path segment (/api/v2/orders), a custom Accept/media-type header, or a request parameter — each with different trade-offs in visibility, cacheability, and routing complexity

the key discipline regardless of mechanism is: never change the meaning of an existing field/endpoint out from under existing clients — add a new version (or a new field) instead, and give clients a clear deprecation window for the old one

springboot.title: Spring Security, JWT & OAuth2
interviewFocus: Design a stateless JWT auth flow end to end
Explain the OAuth2 authorization code flow

questions.text: How do you configure Spring Security in a modern (Spring Boot 3+) app, and how did that change from older versions?
keyPoints: modern Spring Security uses a SecurityFilterChain @Bean built with a lambda DSL (http.authorizeHttpRequests(...).csrf(...).oauth2ResourceServer(...) etc.), instead of extending WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter (deprecated/removed)
this component-based approach also makes it straightforward to define multiple, independently-ordered filter chains for different URL patterns (e.g., stateless API vs a stateful admin UI)

questions.text: Design a stateless JWT authentication flow for a Spring Boot API end to end.
keyPoints: client sends credentials to a login endpoint; the server verifies them and issues a signed JWT (with claims like subject, roles, expiry) instead of creating a server-side session
the client sends that JWT in the Authorization: Bearer header on every subsequent request

a custom filter (added to the SecurityFilterChain before the standard auth filter) validates the token's signature and expiry on each request and populates the SecurityContext — no session lookup needed, which is what makes it horizontally scalable
token revocation before expiry is the classic weak point — mitigated with short expiries + refresh tokens, or a server-side denylist for the rare case

questions.text: In the OAuth2 authorization code flow, what problem does the extra 'code exchange' step solve versus just returning the access token directly to the browser?
keyPoints: the authorization code is short-lived and passed through the browser (less sensitive if intercepted), while the actual access token exchange happens server-to-server (client backend <-> authorization server) using a client secret
this keeps the long-lived, powerful access token out of the browser's history/referrer headers/JS-accessible storage, reducing the attack surface versus the older, now-discouraged implicit flow

questions.text: How do you secure individual service methods (not just URLs) in Spring, and why would you want to?
keyPoints: @EnableMethodSecurity plus annotations like @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") or @PostAuthorize on service methods

URL-level security alone can't express fine-grained rules like 'a user can only edit their OWN order' — method security can evaluate the actual arguments/return value (e.g., @PreAuthorize("#order.ownerId == authentication.name"))

questions.text: How should passwords be stored in a Spring Boot app's database, and what does PasswordEncoder actually do for you?
keyPoints: never store plaintext or reversibly-encrypted passwords — store a one-way salted hash produced by a slow, purpose-built algorithm

Spring Security's PasswordEncoder (BCryptPasswordEncoder by default) handles generating a random salt per password and the hashing/verification, so you never handle raw password bytes yourself beyond the initial comparison call
'slow by design' (BCrypt's work factor) is a deliberate defense against brute-force/rainbow-table attacks on a stolen hash dump — a fast hash like plain SHA-256 would be a mistake here

questions.text: A stateless JWT API is being called from a browser SPA on a different origin. What do you need to configure, and how does it differ from CSRF protection?
keyPoints: CORS: the API must explicitly allow the SPA's origin (via a CorsConfigurationSource / @CrossOrigin) or the browser will block the response before JS ever sees it — this is a browser-enforced same-origin policy concern

CSRF: protects against a malicious site tricking a logged-in user's browser into making unwanted state-changing requests using ambient cookie-based auth — with stateless JWT-in-header auth (not cookies), there's no ambient credential for a forged request to exploit, so CSRF protection is typically disabled for these APIs
conflating the two is a common mistake — disabling CSRF is safe here specifically because auth isn't cookie-based, not because CORS is also configured

springboot.title: Actuator, Observability & Testing
interviewFocus: Why Testcontainers over H2 for a real integration test

questions.text: What does the /actuator/health endpoint actually report, and how is its overall status computed?
keyPoints: it aggregates the status of every registered HealthIndicator (DB connectivity, disk space, message broker connectivity, custom ones you add) into one overall status

the overall status is the WORST of all individual indicator statuses (e.g., if the DB indicator is DOWN, the whole endpoint reports DOWN) — this makes it suitable for load balancer/orchestrator health checks
showDetails/authorization controls how much of that breakdown is exposed publicly vs only to authenticated/internal callers

questions.text: How would you add a custom health check — say, verifying a downstream payment gateway is reachable?
keyPoints: implement the HealthIndicator interface (or HealthContributor) and register it as a bean; Spring Boot Actuator auto-discovers it and folds its result into /actuator/health
the health() method returns Health.up()/.down().withDetail(...) — keep it fast and non-blocking-forever (with a timeout), since a hung health check can itself cause cascading readiness-probe failures

questions.text: What's the difference between a metric exposed via Micrometer and a log line, and why do you generally want both?
keyPoints: metrics are numeric, aggregatable time-series data (request count, latency percentiles, error rate) suited for dashboards/alerting on trends
logs are discrete, detailed event records suited for diagnosing a SPECIFIC failure after an alert fires
Micrometer gives Spring Boot a vendor-neutral metrics facade (like SLF4J does for logging) that can export to Prometheus, Datadog, etc. without changing application code

questions.text: Why reach for Testcontainers rather than an embedded H2 database when writing a Spring Boot integration test against a Postgres-backed service?
keyPoints: H2 doesn't perfectly replicate Postgres's SQL dialect, functions, and constraint-enforcement behavior — a test passing against H2 can still fail against real Postgres in production
Testcontainers spins up the actual Postgres engine in a throwaway Docker container for the test run, so the integration test verifies behavior against the real database technology
the trade-off is a slower test (container startup) versus much higher confidence — typically reserved for a smaller set of true integration tests, not every test

questions.text: What's the difference between @SpringBootTest, @WebMvcTest, and @DataJpaTest, and when would you reach for each?
keyPoints: @SpringBootTest boots the full application context (or close to it) — most realistic but slowest, best for true end-to-end integration tests
@WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers, filters, MockMvc) with collaborators mocked — fast, focused on request/response mapping, validation, and status codes
@DataJpaTest loads only the JPA layer against an in-memory or configured test datasource with transactional rollback per test — fast, focused on repository/query correctness
the general principle: prefer the narrowest slice test that can catch the bug, and reserve @SpringBootTest for the smaller set of tests that genuinely need the whole wiring

questions.text: In a microservices system, how do you trace a single user request as it hops across multiple Spring Boot services, and why doesn't looking at each service's logs separately work well?
keyPoints: each service's logs in isolation show only that service's local view — correlating them by eye across services and timestamps doesn't scale and easily misses the actual causal chain
distributed tracing (e.g., Micrometer Tracing with a backend like Zipkin/Jaeger) propagates a shared trace ID (and per-hop span IDs) through request headers across every service the request touches

this lets you pull up one trace and see the full waterfall — which service was slow, which call failed, and the exact order of downstream calls — instead of manually reconstructing it from scattered logs

springboot.title: Microservices, Messaging & Cloud-Native
objectives: Containerizing & deploying a Spring Boot service
interviewFocus: Design a circuit breaker + fallback for a flaky dependency
Explain the Saga pattern for a distributed 'transaction'
Trace a request through an API gateway to a downstream service

resources.title: Microservices with Spring Boot & Spring Cloud

questions.text: What are the three states of a Resilience4j circuit breaker, and what triggers each transition?
keyPoints: CLOSED: normal operation, requests flow through and failures are counted against a rolling window

OPEN: once the failure rate crosses a configured threshold, the breaker trips — requests fail FAST (immediately, no call to the downstream service) for a wait duration, protecting the failing dependency from more load and freeing up the caller's resources
HALF_OPEN: after the wait duration, a limited number of trial requests are allowed through — if they succeed, the breaker closes again; if they fail, it reopens

questions.text: What problem does the Saga pattern solve for microservices, and how does it work?
keyPoints: a single business operation that spans multiple services (e.g., place an order: reserve inventory + charge payment + schedule shipping) can't use a traditional single-database ACID transaction across service boundaries
a saga breaks it into a sequence of local transactions, each committing in its own service and publishing an event/triggering the next step

if a later step fails, previously completed steps are undone via explicit COMPENSATING actions (e.g., release the inventory reservation) rather than a real rollback — this is eventual consistency, not atomicity

questions.text: Synchronous REST calls vs Kafka-based async messaging between two Spring Boot microservices — what's the real trade-off?
keyPoints: sync REST: simpler mental model, immediate response, but tightly couples the caller's availability/latency to the callee's — if the callee is down or slow, the caller is directly affected

Kafka: decouples producer and consumer completely (the producer doesn't even need the consumer to be running), naturally buffers bursts of load, and enables multiple independent consumers of the same event
the cost is added complexity: eventual consistency, harder request tracing, and needing to reason about message ordering/idempotency/at-least-once delivery

questions.text: What's the role of an API gateway in a microservices architecture, and name two concerns it commonly centralizes.
keyPoints: an API gateway is the single entry point clients call, which routes each request to the correct downstream microservice — clients don't need to know the internal service topology

it commonly centralizes cross-cutting concerns like authentication/authorization, rate limiting, request logging, and response aggregation from multiple services — so individual microservices don't each reimplement them

questions.text: How does a Spring Boot microservice find and call another service by name (e.g., 'order-service') instead of a hardcoded host:port, and why does that matter in a cloud-native environment?
keyPoints: a service registry (Eureka, or the platform's own DNS-based discovery in Kubernetes) tracks which instances of each service are currently alive and where
the calling service resolves the target by logical name through a client-side or platform-level load balancer, which also spreads requests across all healthy instances of that name
this matters because in a cloud-native environment instances are constantly scaling up/down and getting rescheduled to new IPs — hardcoded addresses would break almost immediately

questions.text: What's the practical difference between a retry policy and a bulkhead, and why might combining a retry with a circuit breaker (but no bulkhead) still let one failing dependency take down a whole service?
keyPoints: retry: re-attempts a failed call, useful for transient failures, but blindly retrying a truly-down dependency multiplies load on it and ties up the caller's threads/connections for longer

bulkhead: partitions a limited resource (thread pool, connection pool) per downstream dependency, so one dependency exhausting ITS pool can't starve the threads needed to serve calls to a different, healthy dependency

without a bulkhead, retries against a slow/failing dependency can still exhaust the caller's shared thread pool before the circuit breaker's failure-rate threshold even trips, taking down unrelated request handling in the same service

questions.text: What's the difference between a fat/uber JAR and a Spring Boot layered JAR when it comes to building a Docker image, and why does the layering matter?
keyPoints: a plain fat JAR bundles application code and all dependencies into one monolithic layer — any code change invalidates and re-uploads the entire (often large) image layer

Spring Boot's layered JAR support (spring-boot:build-image, or docker-jar layering) splits the JAR into separate Docker layers — dependencies (which rarely change) in one layer, your actual application classes (which change on every build) in another

Docker caches unchanged layers, so with layering, a routine code change only needs to rebuild/push the small application-code layer instead of the whole image, making builds and deploys significantly faster

git.title: Git Fundamentals
objectives: The three-tree model: working directory, staging area, repository
Commit early, commit often — writing good commit messages
interviewFocus: Explain the working directory / staging area / repository model precisely
Write a commit message that follows convention
Explain why .gitignore doesn't un-track an already-tracked file

questions.text: What are Git's three trees — the working directory, the staging area (index), and the repository (HEAD) — and what does each one actually hold?
keyPoints: the working directory is the actual files on disk that you edit
the staging area (index) is a snapshot-in-progress — the exact set of changes you've told Git you want in the NEXT commit, which can be a subset of everything you've changed
the repository (.git directory, specifically what HEAD points to) holds the permanent, committed history
`git add` copies working-directory changes into the staging area; `git commit` takes whatever is currently staged and seals it into the repository as a new commit

questions.text: What does `git add file.txt` actually do under the hood, and why does that matter for `git diff`?
keyPoints: it computes a hash of the file's current content, stores that content as a blob object in Git's object database, and updates the index to point the file's path at that blob

because staging is a snapshot, plain `git diff` (no args) shows working-directory-vs-staging changes, while `git diff --staged` (or --cached) shows staging-vs-last-commit changes — these are two genuinely different comparisons, not the same diff shown twice
if you edit the file again AFTER staging it, `git add` alone won't include those newest edits in the next commit — you have to re-stage

questions.text: What makes a commit message actually useful six months later, and what's the widely-used convention for structuring one?
keyPoints: a short (~50 char) imperative-mood summary line ('Fix null check in parser', not 'Fixed' or 'Fixes'), a blank line, then an optional body explaining WHY the change was made — the reasoning and trade-offs, not a restatement of the diff itself

the code itself already shows WHAT changed; a good message's whole value is capturing context that isn't visible in the diff — why this approach, what else was considered, what bug or ticket prompted it
conventional commits (feat:, fix:, chore:, etc. prefixes) is one common structured convention that many teams and changelog-generation tools rely on

questions.text: Why doesn't adding a file to .gitignore stop Git from tracking it, if the file was already committed before you added the ignore rule?
keyPoints: .gitignore only tells Git which UNTRACKED files to ignore when deciding what shows up as 'new' — it has no effect on files Git is already tracking

to actually stop tracking it, you need `git rm --cached <file>` (removes it from the repo/index but leaves it on disk) followed by a commit, and only then does the .gitignore rule take effect for it going forward

a common real mistake: committing a secrets file, then adding it to .gitignore and assuming it's now safe — the file (and the secret) is still in the project's history forever unless you separately rewrite history

questions.text: What's the difference between `git log`, `git log --oneline --graph`, and `git show <commit>`, and when would you reach for each?
keyPoints: `git log` gives the full, verbose history — author, date, full message, one commit per block — useful for reading detailed history
`git log --oneline --graph` compresses each commit to one line and draws the branch/merge topology as ASCII art — the fast way to understand HOW branches diverged and merged
`git show <commit>` gives full detail on ONE specific commit, including its actual diff — what to reach for once you've found the commit you care about

questions.text: You ran `git commit` and immediately noticed a typo in the message, with no other changes needed. What's the safe fix, and why is 'safe' conditional here?
keyPoints: `git commit --amend` rewrites the most recent commit (new message, or new content if you also `git add` something first) as an entirely new commit object with a new hash, replacing the old one

it's safe only if that commit hasn't been pushed/shared yet — amending replaces history, so amending a commit others have already pulled creates a divergent history that causes real problems for collaborators on their next pull

git.title: Branching & Merging
objectives: Merge vs squash vs rebase for combining work
interviewFocus: Explain why a Git branch is 'just a movable pointer'
Distinguish a fast-forward merge from a real three-way merge
Resolve a conflict by hand and understand the conflict markers
Pick the right combining strategy for a given situation

questions.text: Why is a Git branch described as 'just a movable pointer to a commit,' and why does that make branching so cheap compared to some older version control systems?
keyPoints: a branch is a tiny file (or ref) holding nothing but a commit hash — creating one is instant and costs almost no disk space, unlike copying an entire codebase
'switching' branches just moves HEAD (and the working directory contents) to point at a different commit — no duplication of the actual project files happens

older systems (like early SVN) often modeled branches as full directory copies, which made branching slow and heavyweight enough that teams avoided it — Git's design specifically optimizes for branching constantly

questions.text: What's the difference between a fast-forward merge and a real three-way merge, and what determines which one Git performs?
keyPoints: fast-forward: happens when the target branch's tip is a direct ancestor of the branch being merged in — Git just moves the pointer forward, no new merge commit is created, and history stays perfectly linear

three-way merge: happens when both branches have diverged (each has commits the other doesn't) — Git compares the two branch tips against their common ancestor and creates a new merge commit with two parents

which one happens is entirely determined by the branch topology, not a flag you set — though `--no-ff` forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward would otherwise be possible, which some teams prefer for a visible record that a feature branch existed

questions.text: You hit a merge conflict and open the file — what do the <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers actually mean, and what must you do before committing?
keyPoints: everything between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is YOUR current branch's version of that section; everything between ======= and >>>>>>> <branch> is the incoming branch's version
you edit the file to keep whichever content (or some combination) is actually correct, and manually delete all three marker lines yourself — Git won't do this part for you
after resolving, `git add` the file to mark the conflict as resolved, then `git commit` to complete the merge — the commit that results is the merge commit itself

questions.text: A feature branch has 15 small, messy 'wip' commits. What's the difference between merging it normally, squash-merging it, and rebasing it onto main first, and which would you pick to keep main's history clean?
keyPoints: a normal merge keeps all 15 commits plus a merge commit in main's history — accurate but noisy
a squash merge combines all 15 commits into a single new commit applied to main — cleanest main history, but loses the individual commit-level history of how the feature was built

rebasing the feature branch onto main first (then fast-forward merging) replays the 15 commits on top of main individually — keeps them as separate commits but makes history linear; often combined with interactive rebase first to also clean up the messy commits themselves
squash-merge is the common choice for exactly this scenario — main only needs to know a coherent feature landed, not every intermediate 'wip' commit along the way

questions.text: What's the practical difference between `git branch -d feature` and `git branch -D feature`?
keyPoints: -d (lowercase) is the SAFE delete — Git refuses if the branch has commits not yet merged into your current branch, preventing accidental loss of unmerged work
-D (uppercase) is a forced delete — it deletes the branch and any of its unmerged commits regardless, with no warning
-D is appropriate when you're certain the branch's work is abandoned or already captured elsewhere (e.g., squash-merged, so the commits technically look 'unmerged' but the content already landed)

questions.text: Two branches modify the SAME line of the SAME file differently. Why does Git flag this as a conflict but not when they modify different lines of the same file?
keyPoints: Git's merge algorithm operates at the line level — it can automatically combine non-overlapping line changes because there's no ambiguity about the final result

when both branches change the identical line differently, there's no automatic way to know which version (or what combination) is 'correct' — that's a judgment call only a human (or explicit merge strategy) can make
this is also why keeping changes small and merging/rebasing frequently reduces conflict pain — the longer two branches diverge, the more likely they touch overlapping lines

git.title: Working with Remotes
interviewFocus: Explain exactly what `git fetch` does that `git pull` doesn't
Explain what a 'tracking branch' actually tracks
Walk through a fork-and-PR contribution end to end

questions.text: What does `git fetch` actually do, and how is that different from `git pull`?
keyPoints: `git fetch` downloads new commits/branches/tags from the remote into your LOCAL copy of the remote-tracking branches (e.g., origin/main) — it never touches your working directory or your local branches

`git pull` is really `git fetch` immediately followed by a merge (or rebase, if configured) of the fetched remote-tracking branch into your current local branch — it DOES change your working directory
fetch is the safer 'see what changed without touching my work' operation — a common workflow is to fetch first, look at what's new, and only then decide to merge/rebase

questions.text: What is a 'tracking branch,' and what convenience does it actually buy you day to day?
keyPoints: a local branch configured to know which remote branch it corresponds to (e.g., local `main` tracks `origin/main`) — set automatically by `git clone` for the default branch, or manually via `git branch --set-upstream-to` or `git push -u`
once set, plain `git push`/`git pull` (no arguments) know exactly which remote branch to talk to, and `git status` can tell you how many commits you're ahead/behind the remote
without a tracking relationship, you'd have to spell out `git push origin my-branch` explicitly every single time

questions.text: Walk through the fork-and-pull-request workflow used by most open-source projects, start to finish.
keyPoints: fork the upstream repo into your own GitHub account (a full server-side copy you control), then `git clone` YOUR fork locally
create a feature branch, make your changes, commit, and `git push` to YOUR fork (not upstream — you typically don't have write access there)
open a pull request from your fork's branch against the upstream repo's branch — maintainers review, request changes, and eventually merge it into upstream
to stay current with upstream while you work, add it as a second remote (commonly named `upstream`) and periodically fetch/merge or rebase your branch onto `upstream/main`

questions.text: You run `git push` and get 'rejected — non-fast-forward.' What does this actually mean, and what's the right way to fix it (versus the dangerous shortcut)?
keyPoints: it means the remote branch has commits that your local branch doesn't have — pushing would silently discard them, so Git refuses to let a normal push do that
the right fix: pull/fetch the remote's new commits and either merge or rebase them into your local branch first, resolving any conflicts, THEN push — this integrates both sets of changes

the dangerous shortcut is `git push --force`, which overwrites the remote branch with your local one, permanently discarding whatever commits were there — reserved for cases like fixing your own not-yet-shared feature branch, and even then `--force-with-lease` is safer since it fails if someone else pushed since you last fetched

questions.text: What's the difference between `origin` and a second remote like `upstream` in a forked-repo setup, and why do you need both?
keyPoints: `origin` conventionally points at YOUR fork (where you have push access) — this is where your feature branches and pushes go
`upstream` points at the original repo you forked from (usually read-only for you) — this is what you fetch/merge from to stay in sync with the project's real progress
without a separate `upstream` remote, you'd have no direct way to pull in the original project's new commits — your fork only updates when YOU push to it

questions.text: What does `git clone` set up automatically that you'd otherwise have to configure by hand?
keyPoints: it creates a local copy of the entire repository history, creates a remote named `origin` pointing back at the source you cloned from, and checks out a local branch (matching the remote's default branch) that already tracks the corresponding `origin/<branch>`
this is why a fresh clone can immediately `git pull`/`git push` with no extra setup — the remote and tracking relationship are already wired up for you

git.title: Rewriting History Safely
objectives: git commit --amend vs git reset vs git revert
Interactive rebase to clean up commits
The reflog as an undo safety net
interviewFocus: Explain how git revert differs fundamentally from git reset
Use interactive rebase to squash/reorder/reword commits
Recover a 'lost' commit using the reflog

resources.title: Git rebase, cherry-pick & reflog deep dive

questions.text: What's the difference between `git reset --soft`, `--mixed`, and `--hard` when moving HEAD back one commit, and what happens to your changes in each case?
keyPoints: --soft: moves HEAD (and the branch pointer) back, but leaves the staging area AND working directory untouched — the old commit's changes now sit fully staged, ready to be recommitted differently
--mixed (the default): moves HEAD back and also resets the staging area to match, but leaves the working directory untouched — the changes are now unstaged, present as regular edits

--hard: moves HEAD back and resets BOTH the staging area and the working directory to match — the changes are gone from disk entirely (recoverable briefly via reflog, but not through normal Git commands)

questions.text: Why is `git revert` considered safe to use on a commit that's already been pushed and shared, while `git reset` on a shared commit is not?
keyPoints: `git revert` creates a BRAND NEW commit that applies the inverse of the target commit's changes — history only grows forward, nothing is deleted or rewritten, so everyone's existing history remains valid and compatible

`git reset` moves the branch pointer backward, literally erasing commits from that branch's history — anyone who already pulled the old history now has a divergent, incompatible view, causing pain on their next pull/push
the rule of thumb: revert (or a fresh commit) for anything already shared; reset is fine for undoing purely local, unpushed work

questions.text: What does `git rebase -i HEAD~4` let you do to your last 4 commits, and name at least three distinct operations available in that interactive editor.
keyPoints: it opens an editable list of the last 4 commits and lets you rewrite that slice of history before it's replayed

pick: keep the commit as-is; reword: keep the changes but edit the commit message; squash (or fixup): combine a commit into the one before it (squash keeps/merges both messages, fixup discards the later one's message); drop: remove a commit entirely; you can also reorder commits simply by reordering the lines
this is the standard way to turn a messy string of 'wip', 'fix typo', 'actually fix it' commits into one or two clean, reviewable commits before opening a pull request

questions.text: What does `git cherry-pick <commit>` do, and give a realistic scenario where you'd reach for it instead of merging or rebasing a whole branch.
keyPoints: it takes the changes introduced by ONE specific commit from anywhere in history and applies them as a new commit on your current branch — without pulling in anything else from that commit's original branch

realistic scenario: a critical bug fix was committed on a `develop` branch, but you need that exact fix on a `release/2.1` branch RIGHT NOW without merging all of develop's other in-progress work into the release branch
cherry-picking creates a genuinely new commit (new hash) with the same changes/message — it's not literally moving the original commit

questions.text: You just ran `git reset --hard` and realize you actually needed one of the commits you just discarded. Is that commit actually gone, and how would you get it back?
keyPoints: it's not immediately gone — Git doesn't garbage-collect unreferenced commits right away, and `git reflog` keeps a local log of every place HEAD has pointed, including the commit you just reset away from

running `git reflog`, finding the commit hash from before the reset, and then `git reset --hard <that-hash>` (or `git cherry-pick`/`git branch recovery <hash>` if you just want the content back) restores it
this only works locally and only for a limited retention window (Git eventually garbage-collects truly unreachable commits) — it's a safety net for recent mistakes, not permanent storage

questions.text: Why is `git commit --amend` considered a special, limited case of rewriting history rather than a routine command to use freely?
keyPoints: it replaces the most recent commit with a brand-new commit object (new hash), which is exactly the same kind of history-rewrite risk as reset/rebase if that commit has already been pushed and pulled by someone else

it's genuinely useful and safe specifically for the narrow case of 'I just committed locally, haven't pushed yet, and want to fix the message or add one forgotten file' — the moment it's shared, the same non-fast-forward problems from rebasing shared history apply

git.title: Team Workflows & Code Review
objectives: Trunk-based development vs Git Flow vs GitHub Flow
Writing a pull request reviewers actually want to review
interviewFocus: Compare trunk-based development, Git Flow, and GitHub Flow and pick the right one for a given team
Structure a pull request for a fast, high-quality review
Explain semantic versioning and how a tag maps to a release
Explain why small, frequent PRs beat large ones

resources.title: A successful Git branching model (Git Flow)

questions.text: Compare trunk-based development, Git Flow, and GitHub Flow — what's the core difference in how long branches live and how often they merge to main?
keyPoints: trunk-based development: everyone commits small, frequent changes directly to (or very short-lived branches merged rapidly into) a single trunk/main — feature flags hide incomplete work rather than long-lived branches

Git Flow: heavyweight, with dedicated long-lived develop/release/hotfix branches alongside main — designed for projects with scheduled, versioned releases (e.g., installed software), but often too much ceremony for continuously-deployed web services

GitHub Flow: a lightweight middle ground — short-lived feature branches off main, opened as a PR, reviewed, and merged straight to main, which is always deployable — the default assumption for most modern continuously-deployed teams

questions.text: What makes a pull request easy and fast for a reviewer to actually review well, versus one that gets rubber-stamped or ignored for days?
keyPoints: small, focused scope — one logical change per PR, not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes, so the reviewer can hold the whole diff's intent in their head
a clear description: WHAT changed and WHY (the reasoning/trade-offs), not just a restatement of the diff — plus how to test it if that's not obvious
self-review first — reading your own diff before requesting review catches the embarrassing stuff (leftover debug prints, commented-out code) before a human has to point it out
a PR that takes an hour to review properly gets skimmed or deferred; a PR that takes ten minutes gets a real, careful review — size is often the single biggest lever a contributor controls

questions.text: What does a Git tag actually mark, and how does semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) communicate what changed in a new release?
keyPoints: a tag is a permanent, named pointer to a specific commit — unlike a branch, it's not meant to move, making it the standard way to mark 'this exact commit is what we shipped as v2.1.0'

MAJOR increments for breaking/incompatible API changes, MINOR for backward-compatible new functionality, PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes — a consumer can tell from the version number ALONE whether upgrading is safe to do blindly (patch/minor) or needs a careful review (major)
an annotated tag (`git tag -a`) additionally stores a message, tagger, and date — the recommended kind for actual releases, versus a lightweight tag which is just a bare pointer

questions.text: How do conventional commit prefixes (feat:, fix:, chore:, BREAKING CHANGE:) enable automated changelog and version-bump tooling?
keyPoints: each prefix has a machine-readable meaning — feat: signals a new feature (typically a MINOR bump), fix: a bug fix (PATCH bump), a BREAKING CHANGE footer signals a MAJOR bump — and chore:/docs:/refactor: etc. mark commits that shouldn't even appear in a user-facing changelog

tooling (like semantic-release) can scan commit history since the last tag, compute the correct next version number automatically from these prefixes, and generate a changelog grouped by category — removing the manual, error-prone, often-skipped step of writing release notes by hand

questions.text: Why do experienced teams strongly prefer many small PRs over one large PR that bundles a whole feature?
keyPoints: review quality drops sharply with diff size — reviewers genuinely can't hold a 2000-line diff's full context in their head, so large PRs get worse review, not more thorough review
a bug found in PR #1 of 5 is cheap to fix immediately; the same bug buried in one giant PR might not surface until much later, after more code has been built on top of the flawed part
small PRs merge faster and more often, which keeps everyone's branches closer to main and reduces the size (and pain) of eventual merge conflicts — this compounds across a whole team

questions.text: In GitHub Flow, main is described as 'always deployable.' What team practices actually make that true, versus it just being an aspirational rule nobody follows?
keyPoints: CI runs the full test suite (and often deploys to staging) on every PR before it's allowed to merge — a PR that breaks the build or tests literally cannot land
incomplete features are hidden behind feature flags rather than left half-built directly in main's code path, so 'merged to main' doesn't have to mean 'fully finished and user-facing yet'

some teams go further with continuous deployment — merging to main automatically triggers a production deploy, which is a strong forcing function: nobody wants to be the one who merges something broken straight to prod

objectives: Bisecting to find the commit that introduced a bug
Submodules vs subtrees for embedding another repo
interviewFocus: Use stash to context-switch without losing work
Run a bisect to pinpoint a regression
Explain the real trade-off between submodules and subtrees
Describe what a pre-commit hook can enforce and why hooks alone aren't a security boundary

questions.text: What does `git stash` actually do, and how is it different from just committing your work-in-progress to switch branches?
keyPoints: it takes your uncommitted changes (staged and/or unstaged) and saves them onto a stack, then restores the working directory to match HEAD — cleanly, without a commit polluting your branch's history
`git stash pop` (or `apply`) restores those changes back later, from any branch — useful for 'I need to urgently switch to fix something else, but I'm not ready to commit this half-finished work'

unlike committing WIP, a stash isn't tied to a specific branch or meant to be shared — it's explicitly a personal, temporary shelf, and stashes can be dropped/lost more easily than commits, so it's not a substitute for real version control of anything you care about long-term

questions.text: How does `git bisect` use binary search to find the exact commit that introduced a regression, and why is that so much faster than checking commits one by one?
keyPoints: you tell it one commit known to be 'good' and one known to be 'bad' (usually HEAD); Git checks out the commit exactly halfway between them and asks you to test and mark it good or bad
each answer halves the remaining range of suspect commits — finding the culprit among, say, 1000 commits takes roughly log2(1000) ≈ 10 tests instead of up to 1000 one-by-one checks
`git bisect run <script>` can automate the whole process if you have a script/test that exits non-zero on the bad state — turning a manual hunt into one command

questions.text: What's the real trade-off between a Git submodule and a Git subtree for embedding one repository inside another?
keyPoints: a submodule stores a POINTER to a specific commit of the external repo — the actual code isn't copied into your repo's history, so your repo stays small, but cloning/updating requires extra submodule-specific commands, and it's a common source of 'why is this folder empty' confusion for contributors who forget `--recurse-submodules`

a subtree actually MERGES the external repo's files and history directly into your repo — contributors get a normal, simple checkout with no extra commands or empty folders, at the cost of your repo's history and size growing to include the embedded project's full history
submodules fit when the dependency genuinely stays external and independently versioned; subtrees fit when you want the embedded code to feel like a normal, native part of your repo

questions.text: What can a Git hook (like pre-commit or pre-push) enforce, and why is it NOT a real security boundary despite looking like one?
keyPoints: hooks are scripts Git runs automatically at specific points (before a commit is created, before a push goes out, etc.) — commonly used to run linters, formatters, or tests, or to block a commit containing an obvious secret pattern

hooks live in the LOCAL .git/hooks directory and are NOT copied when someone clones the repo (by default), and any developer can bypass them entirely with `--no-verify` or by just deleting the hook file — so they're a convenience/consistency tool for cooperative developers, not an enforceable security control

actual enforcement (blocking a secret from ever reaching the remote, requiring passing CI before merge) has to happen server-side — in CI or the hosting platform's branch protection rules — not in a client-side hook alone

questions.text: What problem does Git LFS (Large File Storage) solve, and why does committing large binary files directly to a normal Git repo cause real problems over time?
keyPoints: Git's core design assumes text files that diff and compress efficiently — every version of a large binary (a video, a design file, a dataset) gets stored close to in full in the repo's history, since there's no meaningful line-level diff to compress, so the .git directory balloons and every clone gets slower and heavier forever

Git LFS replaces the large file's content in the repo with a small text pointer, while the actual binary content is stored on a separate LFS server and fetched on demand — this keeps the core repo (and every clone/fetch) small regardless of how many large-file versions have accumulated

the trade-off is dependency on the LFS server being available and correctly configured — an LFS-tracked repo cloned without the extension, or with LFS misconfigured, gives you pointer files instead of the actual assets

questions.text: What does a .gitattributes file control that .gitignore doesn't, and give one concrete, commonly-hit problem it solves.
keyPoints: .gitattributes controls how Git treats specific paths for things like line-ending normalization, diff/merge behavior for particular file types, and marking paths for Git LFS — it's about HOW tracked files are handled, not whether they're tracked at all

concrete example: a cross-platform team hitting constant noisy diffs (or false merge conflicts) purely from CRLF vs LF line-ending differences between Windows and Mac/Linux — a `* text=auto` rule (or explicit per-extension rules) in .gitattributes normalizes line endings consistently on checkin/checkout, eliminating that entire class of noise
